You think you’re just having sex…

But you’re absorbing her regrets, her anger, her bitterness, her loneliness.

That’s why young men who go down this path start acting weird, lost, and confused.

It’s not you — it’s the spiritual residue she dumped on you.

4. YOU AGE SPIRITUALLY WHILE SHE FEELS YOUNGER

She becomes energized.

You become drained.

She gets her youth extended… and you lose yours.

That’s the exchange.

5. YOUR DRIVE AND PURPOSE BEGIN TO DIE

Your goals stop mattering.

Your hunger disappears.

You start settling.

Because she has numbed your ambition with comfort you didn’t earn and attention you didn’t deserve.

6. YOU BECOME HER EMOTIONAL DUMPING GROUND

She confesses old wounds.

Old heartbreaks.

Old resentments.

And you — a young man — carry emotions from a past that isn’t even yours.

7. YOU START LOOKING LOST AND FOOLISH

People can see it.

Your eyes get dull.

Your confidence drops.

Your aura weakens.

You look like a boy tied to a life that doesn’t belong to you.

8. SHE GAINS CONTROL — YOU LOSE YOUR IDENTITY

Once she gets your mind, your spirit, and your ambition wrapped around her comfort,

you stop leading… and start being led.

You think you’re winning — but you’re actually being domesticated.

9. YOU BECOME DEPENDENT ON HER VALIDATION

You stop choosing women your age.

You stop choosing growth.

You stop choosing challenge.

Because she made you addicted to the easy life.

10. YOUR FUTURE RELATIONSHIPS SUFFER

You carry her chaos into your next chapter.

You become confused, insecure, ungrounded — because you gave your youth to a woman who had already lived hers.

11. YOU BREAK YOUR OWN DESTINY FOR TEMPORARY COMFORT

Your twenties are supposed to build your empire.

Sleeping with older women destroys that focus.

You’re exchanging your future for a moment of escape.

12. THE SPIRITUAL DEBT LASTS LONGER THAN THE AFFAIR

Her touch fades.

Her money finishes.

Her attention moves on.

But the damage stays.

Your spirit will need years to cleanse what she left behind.

FINAL WARNING

Men, never trade your destiny for comfort.

Never exchange your youth for validation.

Never let loneliness push you into the arms of a woman carrying decades of emotional storms.

Older women are not a shortcut — they are a spiritual trap.

Protect your energy, or you’ll wake up one day drained, directionless, and wondering where your fire went.

Choose growth over comfort.

Choose your future over her loneliness.

Choose discipline over destruction.

Historically, white people were not the only group to harbor anti-Black prejudice. This becomes clear through the study of Arab and Islamic history, where anti-Black attitudes and the enslavement of Black people existed long before the transatlantic slave trade.

The belief that certain peoples had the right to own, enslave, or dominate Black people dates back centuries. The story of Bilal ibn Rabah offers an important example of how race, slavery, and religion intersected in early Islamic history.

This pattern was not limited to one region or group. European history includes the Doctrine of Discovery, Portuguese and Spanish royal laws and ordinances, English colonial laws especially the Virginia slave codes and papal bulls such as Dum Diversas (1452). Islamic societies also developed legal systems regulating slavery, including the enslavement.

Long before the transatlantic slave trade, the enslavement and dehumanization of Black people already existed.

We often forget how deep this history goes. The story is bigger than any one group. It is about understanding the historical systems that repeatedly treated Black people as people who could be conquered, enslaved, or controlled. Both Christianity and Islam have been used to control Black people, and institutions associated with both religions participated in systems of enslavement. In some places, religious teachings were also used to justify or regulate forms of slavery that continued to affect Black communities long after formal abolition.

This ancient war never  ended.

text:
🚨 THE GRAVE IS NOT GOD'S DEADLINE.

CHRIST PREACHED TO THE DEAD. PAUL MENTIONED BAPTISM FOR THEM. THE RESTORATION EXPLAINS WHY.

Billions have died without hearing the name of Jesus Christ, reading a Bible, or receiving His ordinances.

Does their opportunity disappear because they were born in the wrong century or on the wrong continent?

Peter gives a startling answer.

CHRIST CROSSED THE VEIL

Christ was put to death in the flesh, made alive by the Spirit, and preached to the spirits in prison, including those disobedient in the days of Noah. 1 Peter 3:18-20.

Peter then says the gospel was preached to the dead so they could be judged according to mortal life but live according to God in the spirit. 1 Peter 4:6.

Some interpret that second passage as referring to people who heard the gospel while alive and later died. That interpretation is possible, but the verse itself does not say it, and it does not erase Christ preaching to imprisoned spirits in the previous chapter.

Many Christians preserved Christ's descent into the realm of the dead.

They preserved the trip and misplaced the mission.

PAUL LEFT THE ORDINANCE IN PLAIN SIGHT

Paul asks why people are baptized for the dead if the dead do not rise. 1 Corinthians 15:29.

The verse does not provide an ordinance manual. Paul says they rather than we, so the passage alone does not prove every detail of modern temple practice.

But it proves something critics often pretend is not there.

Baptism for the dead existed among people known to Paul's audience, and Paul used it to support the resurrection. He did not interrupt his argument to condemn it as paganism, heresy or nonsense.

Paul did not accidentally leave a Mormon Easter egg in the resurrection chapter.

THE WIDER SCRIPTURAL RECORD REMEMBERS

Second Maccabees 12 records Judas Maccabeus collecting money for an offering on behalf of fallen soldiers. The author calls prayer for the dead reasonable because he believes they will rise again and describes making atonement for them.

That is not baptism for the dead. It is evidence that pre-Christian Jews could believe the living might act religiously for the benefit of the dead.

Second Maccabees remains in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles but sits outside the Protestant 66-book collection. Closing the canon does not make the older witness disappear.

Then the second-century Shepherd of Hermas describes deceased apostles and teachers preaching to people who died before them and giving them the seal through water. A modern scholarly analysis identifies the scene as postmortem baptism for righteous people who lived before Christ.

The Shepherd of Hermas is not part of our canon, and it does not establish doctrine by itself.

It does establish history.

The idea that the dead could hear Christ's message and receive baptismal benefit did not fall from the Utah sky in the nineteenth century.

THE JUSTICE PROBLEM

God is no respecter of persons. Acts 10:34.

He desires all people to be saved and come to a knowledge of the truth. 1 Timothy 2:4.

Yet countless people never received that knowledge during mortality.

If death permanently closes every opportunity, salvation partly depends upon geography, historical timing, childhood survival and whether the correct missionary reached your village.

That turns Providence into roulette.

THE RESTORATION MAKES THE FRAGMENTS WHOLE

Doctrine and Covenants 138 explains that Christ entered the spirit world and organized righteous messengers to carry the gospel to those in darkness.

The dead are taught faith in Christ, repentance and the ordinances performed vicariously for them.

Nobody is forced to accept anything.

Proxy baptism preserves both divine justice and human agency. The ordinance is offered among the living. The individual remains free to accept or reject it among the dead.

That is why the hearts of the children turn to their fathers. Malachi 4:5-6.

That is why Paul says the faithful dead cannot be made perfect without us. Hebrews 11:39-40.

A Christ who conquered death is not stopped by a funeral.

The restored gospel proclaims the complete apostolic doctrine: Christ's gospel reaches the dead, His saving ordinances are offered without coercion, families can be sealed across death, and Jesus Christ remains Lord on both sides of the veil.

text:
The world is the organized system that operates independently of God and opposes His truth. It has its ambitions, fashions, philosophies, entertainment, morality, religion, heroes, and rewards. Satan is called “the god of this world” who blinds the minds of unbelievers (2 Corinthians 4:4), and Ephesians 2:2 calls him “the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience.” The world pressures the believer from without; the flesh pulls from within; the devil schemes against him through both. A Christian may resist a direct lie from the enemy while still surrendering to an appetite of the flesh. He may avoid obvious immorality while becoming intoxicated with the pride and applause of the world. Therefore, resistance involves more than rebuking a spiritual opponent. It includes refusing conformity to the world and refusing to yield the body to sin.

Recognizing these distinctions prevents superstition. If the problem is the flesh, the biblical answer includes reckoning oneself dead to sin, refusing to yield one’s members, fleeing youthful lusts, and walking in the Spirit. If the pressure comes through the world, the believer must reject its friendship, values, and conformity. If the devil presents a lie, accusation, snare, or fiery dart, the Christian must resist steadfastly in the faith. Often all three are involved, and the same act of obedience addresses them together. The believer does not need an elaborate ceremony to determine which percentage of a temptation originated from which enemy. He needs truth, submission, watchfulness, prayer, and obedience. Doctors may argue over the Latin name of the infection, but if the house is on fire, it is a good time to locate the extinguisher. The Bible supplies the necessary diagnosis and the required weapons.

8. Jesus Resisted the Devil With the Written Word

Matthew 4 and Luke 4 provide the perfect pattern of resistance. Satan approached Jesus after He had fasted forty days and was hungry. The first temptation targeted a legitimate physical appetite: “If thou be the Son of God, command that these stones be made bread” (Matthew 4:3). Hunger was not sinful, and making bread was not beyond Christ’s power. The temptation was to act independently of the Father’s will at Satan’s suggestion. Jesus answered, “It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.” Christ did not deny His hunger; He placed obedience above appetite. Submission to the Father came before resistance against the devil. He would rather remain hungry within the will of God than eat a satanically suggested meal outside it. The first Adam ate in a garden full of food and fell. The last Adam refused food in a wilderness and stood.

In the second temptation, Satan quoted Scripture. He cited Psalm 91 while urging Christ to cast Himself from the pinnacle of the temple. This reveals that merely hearing Bible words does not prove that the speaker is serving God. Satan can quote a verse, omit its balance, twist its application, and use it to promote presumption. Jesus answered, “It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God” (Matthew 4:7). Scripture must interpret Scripture. A promise of protection does not authorize foolishness or disobedience. The word “again” is vital. One passage cannot be isolated from the remainder of divine revelation and made to teach something contrary to the whole. The devil has filled pulpits with men who can quote a verse but cannot rightly divide the word of truth. They use isolated promises like loaded dice, always managing to throw the number that benefits their program.

In the final temptation, Satan offered the kingdoms of the world in exchange for worship. Jesus commanded, “Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve” (Matthew 4:10). Then the devil left Him. Luke 4:13 says, “And when the devil

Hugues looked at the twelve. “If the house is real, I can call more galleys, as well as men still on Cyprus who remember how to fight. And weapons that are not listed in any prior’s roll.”
The Bruce — he used his name then — nodded. “Then call them. Edward of England is not done. He has smelled what crosses the water. He too is looking for what you once guarded.”
They trained in the short light of an encroaching winter. Wet grass. A line that broke on purpose and formed again behind a fold of land. The rank and file of both chess and battle, and long pointed sticks raised from a ditch. How to read a field and win the war before the first arrow was loosed. How to leave a camp that looked like no one had slept. It was the guerilla warfare that the Holy Land had taught after the first glory had died.
One evening on the machair the king brought it up, “They say your first Master buried a thing at Temple. They say Becket knew a word and took it to heaven with him. My priests talk in circles about a secret that was lost. But I need horsemen, not riddles.”
“The riddle is why men still come,” Hugues said. “We did not find it. Your Tironensian priests did not find it. We will continue the search with them, but for now what we can give you is not the stone. It is the rule we once lived by, and we would like to live it again. For my men will conquer, or die.”
In the hut they did what the Order no longer allowed. No papal bull. No chapter in Paris. Twelve men initiated a hunted king. The new grand master of a new order. Hugues spoke the old vows, of poverty that meant they would eat what the land gave; obedience to the new order and to the man who had offered the shore; a fight that was not Acre and not Cyprus. They gave it a new name - a new royal order of Scotland founded on Icolmkill - because the old name would get them hanged when the letters from France arrived. The clerk wrote nothing down.
“If this holds,” Bruce said, “it holds after the next battle as well as this winter.”
They did not speak of Bannockburn for that name was not yet born. Hugues said only, “A rule is confirmed by remaining.”
News came in fragments, the way news comes to islands. Edward Plantagenet was moving north again with a host and a question: what had crossed from the eastern sea, and what where they after? The old king had spent his life breaking Scots and would spend the last of it trying to own the one true stone. Hugues believed that part. He did not need to believe that Scotland deserved its freedom. Powerful men invent reasons after they have already decided to ride.
Another fragment: the King of France was counting his Templar gold and finding the total insufficient for his wars. Philip did not need a grail stone to hate an Order that answered to no crown. He needed debt and a weak pope. And a house refounded beyond his reach would certainly not make him any kinder.
The clerk asked, at the end of a black afternoon, whether they were still Templars.
Hugues folded the white mantle and put it back in the chest.
“We are what was left when the Temple became an office,” he said. “The thing Payens brought is not in our chest. If it ever sat at Balantrodoch, it is not sitting for us. We came for a shore and a king who needs us. That is our house now.”
Outside, Icolmkill took the weather. Far south in Paris, clerks were already sharpening charges that would be read on Friday the 13th. Hugues slept with his sword inside the blanket, as he once did in the desert. In the morning he would send word to Cyprus: a home existed; the galleys could come; the work was to keep a hunted man alive long enough for a new kingdom to remember it had one.
The centre of the circle, if it had ever existed, stayed lost. The watch did not

text:
UNITED $UAL PROMISED TO WIN BACK 100% OF THE OIL SHOCK BY DECEMBER:

United Airlines at $105.87, -$3.09 / -2.84% today. The Chicago company, founded 1968 and running 113,200 people, flies passengers and cargo worldwide. It opened this morning at $109.58 - the high of its day - and has given back every cent of that and more since.

The verdict: United has already told the market how this is supposed to end. In July it said it would recover 80% to 90% of the oil shock through fares in the third quarter, and 100% of it by the fourth. That promise was priced off a barrel that no longer exists, and today is the market marking the difference.

Start with the barrel, because it is dated and specific. Saudi Arabia shut its East-West pipeline on Friday after drone strikes, and regional officials put the repair at three to five weeks. That line was built in the 1980s to carry roughly 7M barrels a day to the Red Sea without passing the Strait of Hormuz - the exact detour the world now cannot use. Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, is above $107 a barrel, a four-month high and about 2% above Monday's $105.34 settle. The United States Oil Fund, USO, the ordinary way to own that move in a brokerage app, is at $160.58, +$3.92 / +2.50% today.

Now the part that reaches people who never buy a barrel. The US 10-year Treasury yield - the annual interest Washington pays to borrow for a decade, and the rate most mortgages and company bonds are priced against - reached 5.02% today, its highest since 2007. The Federal Reserve announces Wednesday at 2:00pm ET, and futures markets are heavily positioned for a quarter-point increase, which would be the first rise since 2023. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust, SPY, is at $756.86, -$4.02 / -0.53%.

Put those together and the session explains itself. A central bank can raise the price of money. It cannot refill a pipeline. So the barrel does as it likes, the Fed tightens into it, and the squeeze lands on the same household United is counting on to pay a higher fare.

Here is what that fuel line has already done to this company. July 15, for the three months to June 30:

- Revenue $17.67B, +16%
- Aircraft fuel $5.11B, +84.1% - 30.8 cents of every dollar United spent
- Fuel price $4.19 a gallon, +79.4%
- Net income $805M, -17.3%; diluted profit $2.46 a share

Revenue grew 16% and profit fell 17%. One line did that, and it is the one line management does not set.

Which is why the recovery promise is the only number that matters here. United built its third-quarter map on jet fuel at about $3.69 a gallon, taken from the Gulf Coast forward curve as of July 14. It had just paid $4.19 in the quarter that ended two weeks earlier. The assumption sat below what the company had already been charged - and that was before anyone shut a pipeline.

Management was candid about the drift. In that same July update it said fuel costs had risen $575M since early July, or $1.12 a share, for the third quarter alone. Its guide for the quarter is $2.50 to $3.50 a share. Analysts carry $3.19 - the top third of a range resting on a fuel price the market has since overtaken.

United is a current pick on none of the six Len5es, and the cheapest-looking fact about it is the reason. At about 10.2 times the last year of profit it screens like a bargain to both value styles - one hunting a business almost nobody could rebuild bought under its worth, the other hunting settled earning power bought cheaply - but neither is offered settled earnings here, because this profit is the residue left after a fuel bill the company does not price, and 2.12 times book value - what owners would keep if everything were sold and every debt paid - is no discount besides. The Momentum Len5 wants a price near the top of its own one-year range with the recent climb and the longer one agreeing, and $105.87 sits 23.7% under the $138.77 of June 30. The Income Len5 needs a cheque, and United pays no dividend at all. CHANGE IT: two or three years of profit landing in the same neighborhood, which is precisely what an airline cannot show while the barrel moves like this.

Copa Holdings at $125.23, -$2.26 / -1.77% today, is what this looks like once the recovery has already failed. The Panama City carrier, founded 1947, flies across the Americas through a single hub. In its June quarter revenue rose 25.7% to $1.06B while profit per share fell 53.9% to $1.67, on all-in jet fuel of $4.28 a gallon, up 85%. It is a current pick on the Income Len5, sixteenth of thirty, on $1.71 a share paid today - about 5.3% a year - and it sits sixteenth rather than higher because that cheque has the thinnest cover and the heaviest borrowings behind it of any name that Len5 is watching.

WATCH the recovery percentage, not the revenue line. Fares rising is not the test. Fares rising faster than the fuel bill is the test, and United has published the exact figure it expects to clear. WHEN: third-quarter results are confirmed for Tuesday, October 20, after the close. RISK: the whole promise assumes a traveller who keeps paying, and tomorrow afternoon the Fed sets about making that traveller's mortgage, car loan and credit card dearer.

United's answer to a barrel it cannot control was a forecast - and then it published the gallon price the forecast rests on. That is unusually specific for a guide, and it leaves the company nowhere to stand: the fuel price is public, the recovery target is public, and by December one of the two will have been wrong.

Not investment advice.

text:
Why we must prepare for the Chinese Communist Party’s collapse. Successful post-totalitarian reconstruction requires ready plans

The greatest strategic challenge posed by China may not be what happens if the Chinese Communist Party succeeds, but what happens if it suddenly fails. For decades, Western policy has been almost entirely devoted to managing the CCP as a permanent feature of international life: deterring its military aggression, countering its economic coercion, protecting technology, defending Taiwan and competing with Beijing for global influence.

Far less attention has been paid to a different possibility: the sudden collapse of communist rule itself.

That is a dangerous failure of imagination. History repeatedly demonstrates that seemingly permanent dictatorships can disappear with astonishing speed. In 1989, six communist governments in Eastern Europe fell within months. The Berlin Wall, perhaps the most imposing physical symbol of the Cold War, fell almost overnight. Two years later, the Soviet Union itself vanished.

As the Hudson Institute report “China after Communism: Preparing for a Post-CCP China” argues, the People’s Republic of China has survived many crises, but the sudden collapse of the world’s longest-ruling communist dictatorship and second-largest economy is hardly inconceivable.

The international consequences would be enormous. China is not merely another authoritarian country. It possesses nuclear weapons, the world’s largest standing military by personnel, enormous security and intelligence organizations, advanced biological laboratories, vast state enterprises, major financial institutions and supply chains embedded throughout the world economy.

The collapse of central authority could therefore create simultaneous military, financial, humanitarian, political and proliferation crises.

Who controls the nuclear arsenal? Who commands the People’s Liberation Army? What becomes of the People’s Armed Police, the militia, the Ministry of State Security and the vast domestic surveillance apparatus? Who secures dangerous biological facilities? Who prevents provincial military commanders or security chiefs from becoming warlords? What happens to the renminbi, China’s banks, sovereign obligations, state enterprises, foreign reserves and trillions of dollars of domestic assets?

Then come the political questions. What happens in Tibet and Xinjiang — ethnic vengeance or immediate declaration of independence? What becomes of Hong Kong? How should a new government deal with Taiwan? What to do with the 100 million CCP members? How should the crimes of the Mao-to-Xi era — Tiananmen, religious persecution, mass surveillance, forced labor and other abuses — be investigated without turning justice into vengeance?
These are not theoretical questions to be answered after the collapse. After the collapse may already be too late.

The central lesson of 20th-century regime transitions is that preparation matters.

Central and Eastern Europe offer important examples — and important contrasts. Poland entered its decisive transition with something Russia conspicuously lacked: an organized civil society capable of becoming an alternative center of political legitimacy. Solidarity had spent years building networks of intellectuals, workers, economists, lawyers, clergy and political activists.

By 1989, serious debates were already taking place among Solidarity-associated economists about monetary stabilization, ownership, markets and the transition to a market economy. The eventual Balcerowicz reforms were extraordinarily rapid and painful, but they emerged within a political transition possessing organized opposition, popular legitimacy and an increasingly clear institutional destination.

Czechoslovakia possessed Charter 77 and a network of dissidents who had spent years thinking about human rights, political responsibility, historical truth and the moral foundations of government. When communist authority collapsed, those networks supplied Vaclav Havel and the Civic Forum with experienced people, trusted relationships and political legitimacy.

East Germany similarly developed civic movements, and once the regime began to disintegrate, opposition groups and the crumbling party structure together created a Central Round Table that immediately addressed free elections, the dissolution of the secret police apparatus, democratic transformation and even the drafting of a new constitution. Its first meeting, on Dec. 7, 1989, established, among other subcommittees, a working group to begin drafting a new constitution. 

The lesson is not that these transitions were painless. They were not. The lesson is that successful post-totalitarian reconstruction requires institutions, people, principles and plans ready before the political vacuum becomes catastrophic. Russia demonstrates the alternative. The Soviet state collapsed before Russia had developed comparable democratic institutions, an independent civil society capable of governing, a broadly legitimate system for privatizing state property or a durable constitutional consensus.

Economic transformation consequently became entangled with political improvisation, oligarchic acquisition of public wealth, institutional weakness and eventually nationalist authoritarianism.
zoom-in.

Russian President Vladimir Putin did not restore Soviet communism; he exploited the institutional wreckage left by its collapse.

Ukraine likewise inherited many Soviet structures: networks of corruption, oligarchic power and weak institutions. It spent decades struggling to build a more accountable democratic state. These experiences should warn us against assuming that removing a dictatorship automatically produces democracy.

China would present these problems on a vastly greater scale.

The Hudson report, therefore, correctly treats post-CCP planning as a matter of strategic prudence. It examines securing dangerous facilities, stabilizing the financial system, privatizing state assets, restructuring the PLA and security services, protecting vulnerable populations, opening secret-police archives, establishing truth-and-reconciliation mechanisms, and eventually convening a constitutional process.

America has a special responsibility — and a unique capacity — to prepare.

The U.S. has repeatedly demonstrated that defeating or surviving a dictatorship is only half the strategic task. After 1945, America did not simply celebrate the destruction of Nazi Germany and Imperial Japan and go home.

Along with its allies and the peoples of those countries, it helped demilitarize former enemies, rebuild institutions, revive economies, establish constitutional government and transform two militaristic dictatorships into prosperous democracies, ultimately becoming close American allies.

In Japan, the occupation explicitly pursued demilitarization and democratization, helping establish the postwar constitutional order. With those historical precedents in mind, the U.S. should begin that planning now — not to dictate China’s future or impose an American government on the Chinese people. China’s future belongs to the Chinese people.

Still, America, Japan, Taiwan, Europe, Australia, South Korea, India and other democracies have an enormous interest in preventing the collapse of communist rule from producing civil war, nuclear proliferation, economic catastrophe, ethnic violence or another dictatorship.

Washington should establish a permanent interagency planning mechanism for a post-CCP contingency and begin working quietly with allies, Chinese democrats, economists, constitutional scholars, dissidents, religious leaders, overseas Chinese communities and specialists in transitional justice.

The Hudson report recommends in-advance American planning and an interagency task force rather than assuming another relatively peaceful 1989 will simply happen by itself.

Plans should exist for securing strategic weapons, stabilizing financial markets, maintaining essential services, protecting archives, preventing mass reprisals, dismantling political police organizations, separating the military from the CCP, establishing legitimate privatization procedures, recovering stolen public assets, creating truth-and-reconciliation mechanisms and helping Chinese citizens construct a constitutional order. 

The report correctly emphasizes that economic privatization without democratic legitimacy risks becoming little more than the transfer of national wealth to politically connected elites. The objective should not be an Americandesigned China. It should be to give the Chinese people the greatest possible opportunity to build their own free, peaceful, constitutional China. 

The West spent 40 years preparing to defeat Soviet communism but remarkably little time preparing for the morning after it disappeared. We were fortunate that much of Central Europe had prepared itself. We should not depend on such good fortune again. The CCP may survive for decades, or it may collapse with the breathtaking speed of the communist regimes of 1989. We cannot know when, but history gives us no excuse for being surprised twice.

Readying for China after communism is not a regimechange policy. It is insurance against the most consequential political contingency of the 21st century.

Miles Yu is the director of the China Center at the Hudson Institute. His “Red Horizon” column appears every other Tuesday in The Washington Times. He can be reached at mmilesyu@gmail.com.

text:
I am 100 percent Canadian. That makes me 100 percent North American. 🇨🇦🇺🇸🇲🇽Not European. Not “the most European of non-European countries.” Zero percent Brussels. Zero percent Strasbourg talking points.

Name one country on earth that would not want Canada’s geographic position: a shared continent, an integrated industrial base, and an imaginary line between us and the largest, richest market in the world. That is not a slogan. That is the country we actually live in.Carney can sell the European line to a room that already wants to hear it. His supporters will nod because it lets them feel worldly without looking at a map. They treat Canada like a finishing school for European manners: same flag, different continent, different neighbours, different problems. They lecture about values while the country that trades, works, freezes, and pays the bills on this side of the Atlantic is treated as an embarrassment to be managed.

Then they act shocked by the arithmetic.

About 72 percent of Canada’s goods exports still go to the United States. In some recent months that share has fallen into the mid-60s, not because Ottawa discovered a new continent, but because the relationship is being broken on purpose. Roughly three-fifths of our merchandise imports still come from the U.S. The honest point is simpler: we need that market far more than it needs ours. A trade war with your largest customer is not courage. It is a bet that slogans can replace customers.

Walking away from talks at the eleventh hour does not change that. Here is what happened. After weeks of negotiations, the talks collapsed late on the deadline. Washington said it had offered Canada the most preferential treatment of any major exporter. Ottawa said the last-minute terms were a bad deal, suspended negotiations, and sent its team home. Fine. Argue the terms. Do not pretend Canada can casually replace three-quarters of its export market with Europe and a press release.

And do not rewrite the scoreboard of that night. Foolish Liberals cheered as if Carney had just bodychecked the big bad orange man. Elbows up. Never 51. A hockey slogan instead of a customer.

More than eleven years ago, the United States was not treated as an enemy. It was treated as a partner. That is the relationship this country was built on. Now the same crowd that cannot look at a map wants to pick a fight with the market that keeps the lights on.

And do not even get me started on the outrageous immigration taking place while all of this is happening.

Some of us look at the pattern and draw a harder conclusion. Carney is in cahoots with Trump to cripple Canada until the only option left is for the United States to annex us. For me, it cannot happen soon enough. I am 100 percent Canadian. That makes me 100 percent North American.

Do not rewrite the economic scoreboard either. Canada was the only G7 country, and for a stretch the only G20 country, to slip into a technical recession: two straight quarters of shrinking GDP in late 2025 and early 2026. Growth has since ticked back up. That does not erase the damage: weak per-capita growth, businesses getting hit, companies uprooting to the States, and households falling further behind.

Meanwhile Ottawa boasts of more than $26 billion in aid to Ukraine since 2022. Food Banks Canada recorded nearly 2.2 million visits in a single month — the highest number they have ever counted. Visits have more than doubled since 2019. One in four people in this country now lives with food insecurity. You can support Ukraine and still notice that Canadians are lining up for groceries. A government that cannot hold both thoughts at once is not serious.

If the Canada they want is a European talking point with a maple-leaf sticker, they should say so. Stop wrapping a transatlantic rebrand in patriotism while the North American advantage — the one thing almost every other country would kill for — is being talked away.

Bob Russell

text:
BRANIFF HISTORY TODAY - On this day, Friday, September 15, 1972, Braniff International inaugurated Non-Stop service from the Houston Gateway to Acapulco, Mexico, and Non-Stop from the Dallas Gateway to Mexico City and Acapulco. The new flights were the first Non-Stop flights ever offered from Dallas.

Before the route award, Braniff flights were required to stop at San Antonio, Texas, before proceeding to Mexico. Braniff first served Mexico beginning with service to Mexico City from San Antonio in 1960, with service added to Acapulco in December 1965. Aerovias Braniff, a Mexico-based airline owned by Braniff cofounder and President Thomas Elmer Braniff was authorized to fly DC-3s from Nuevo Laredo to Mexico City beginning in 1945. However, because of interference from Pan American World Airways and its influence with the Mexican Government, service was discontinued in early 1946.

Braniff Airways was first authorized by the Civil Aeronautics Board to fly between Mexico City and Panama City/Balboa City, in the Canal Zone in an award of 7719-miles of routes between the US Mainland and Mexico, Cuba and Central and South America in May 1946. However, because of negotiations with Mexico service was not allowed until 1960.

The new 1972 flights greatly enhanced tourism between the United States and Mexico. Braniff would operate 35 weekly flights between the Gateway cities of Houston, Dallas, and San Antonio. Through-plane service was available from the Rocky Mountains, east, Midwest, south, and southwest via these Gateway cities to the two Mexico destinations.

On September 14, 1972, a group of 100 civic and business leaders arrived at Dallas Love Field to fly on a special preinaugural flight from Dallas to Acapulco, Mexico. The Boeing 727 flight departed Love Field at 330PM with Braniff executives on board to host the flight. Braniff Executive Vice President John J. Casey and Charles S. South, Vice President of South America, enjoyed the new Non-Stop service along with the 100 VIP passengers on board. Local city officials on the flight included Dallas City Secretary Harold G. Shank and Ft Worth Mayor R. M. Stovall.

Upon arrival at Acapulco the inaugural party was greeted by Braniff officials including Flavio Manzi, George Salvans, and Acapulco's society guru and Braniff travel doyenne Ms. Sloan Simpson. Simpson was the former First Lady of New York who had traveled to Acapulco in the 1950s and made the resort her home in 1960. In 1967, Sloan was hired by Braniff International to head the company's new "Call Sloan" campaign. Customers could Call Sloan at the Braniff office, upon arrival at Acapulco, and find out anything they wanted to know about the city, "Where the Jetset Turn Off Their Motors."

The preinaugural guests were treated to a dinner at Tres Vidas, a resort villa developed by longtime Braniff shareholder and Board Member Troy Victor Post. Later in the evening, they enjoyed a spectacular firework display, which was the perfect close to an exciting day. The guests were enthralled with Acapulco, as well as Braniff's new service, which coincided with the September 16, 1972, celebration of Mexico's Independence.

On September 15, the first Non-Stop flight from Acapulco to Houston Intercontinental Airport was flown with special guest dignitaries from Mexico on board. Braniff President C Edward Acker and Vice President Tom Robertson of Route and Regulatory Proceedings, flew from Dallas to Houston to greet the arriving first scheduled flight with guests that included Mexico's Undersecretary Mario Ramon Beteta. The Undersecretary was sent to represent the President of Mexico during Houston's celebration of Mexico Independence Day.

A wonderful reception and scrumptious buffet dinner was served at the famed Warwick Hotel which was hosted by Braniff and the Mexico National Tourist Council. Also attending the special event were 150 Houston dignitaries, business and civic leaders, and Mayor Louie Welch.

text:
5 Great American Bike Rides of 25 Miles or Less

Whether you’re looking for a soothing seaside cruise or a blood-pumping Rocky Mountain ascent, these rides are perfect for a spectacular day trip.

From a wildflower-lined path along the California coast to the tree tunnels of a rail trail in New York, you can see a lot of America’s most beautiful places on a bike.

These five rides, all 25 miles or less, offer a variety of landscapes and difficulty levels. Four are paved, one is gravel, and all are car-free. Some don’t even require a vehicle to get to the beginning.

Many of these trails also offer opportunities for camping, wildlife viewing, bird watching and swimming, so you might want to plan for frequent rest stops.

1. CALIFORNIA
Pacific Grove to Fort Ord Dunes State Park
The Monterey Bay Coastal Recreation Trail skirts the dunes and beaches of the Monterey Peninsula on the Central Coast of California.

This paved 20-mile out-and-back ride along the Monterey Bay Coastal Recreation Trail winds among the landmarks and rugged shorelines of the Monterey Peninsula. From Lovers Point Park, you’ll pass Monterey Bay Aquarium; Cannery Row, the former sardine-canning waterfront district famous from John Steinbeck’s 1945 novel of the same name; and Old Fisherman’s Wharf, where sea lions sunbathe in the fishy air. Views of the Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary commingle with cypress trees and birdsong. 

As you sweep around the bay, the path offers flourishes of purple lupines, beach primrose and Indian paintbrush, and bluff-top overlooks of Monterey State Beach and Fort Ord Dunes State Park. As you revel in the laid-back California vibe, you may find yourself pondering this line from “Cannery Row”: “Being at ease with himself put him at ease with the world.”

2. WYOMING
Moose to Jenny Lake
The Grand Teton Pathway gives riders access to breathtaking views without leaving them out of breath.

Some rides make you work for an epic view, but this one delivers jaw-dropping mountain vistas with only a gentle incline. From the Craig Thomas Discovery & Visitor Center, half a mile from the main Moose Entrance station at Grand Teton National Park, follow the paved multiuse Grand Teton Pathway for about eight miles. 

As you pedal through a glacier-carved valley with alpine meadows and sagebrush flats, the jagged Teton Range remains your constant companion. At the Jenny Lake Visitor Center, consider parking your bike and taking a boat across the lake.

3. COLORADO
Frisco to Vail Pass
The Ten Mile Recreational Pathway climbs from Frisco, Colo., to the 10,662-foot summit of Vail Pass, for riders seeking more of a challenge.

Colorado excels at dreamy high-altitude rides, and this paved, 24-mile out-and-back excursion with 1,500 feet of elevation gain is sure to leave its imprint on you. This classic high-country trip heads out from Frisco on the Ten Mile Recreational Pathway, offering a visual feast with a Tour de France-caliber climb. Through Copper Mountain and up the east side of Vail Pass, take in the quaking aspens and whispering streams. 

But stay alert for e-bikers and wildlife like marmots and mountain goats. The path gets steep after Copper Mountain, with the average grade reaching around 7 percent on some final switchbacks up to the Vail Pass summit, at 10,662 feet. If you’d rather skip the ascent, Pioneer Sports and Rebel Sports, in Frisco, offer shuttle service (and bike rentals) to the top of the pass, so you can coast down instead. Whatever you do, the best postride reward is a Final Summit saison at Outer Range Brewing Co in Frisco.

4. NEW YORK
Millerton to Copake Falls
The Harlem Valley Rail Trail runs through the peaceful village of Millerton, N.Y., about 11 miles north of the Metro-North commuter rail stop in Wassaic.

Rolling north from the village of Millerton on this paved, 25-mile out-and-back section of the Harlem Valley Rail Trail, you’ll quickly find yourself immersed in purple phlox, marshlands, farms, forests and the curves of the Taconic Range. First imagined in the mid-1980s on the abandoned bed of the Harlem Railroad, the trail features tree tunnels, basking water snakes, turtles and busy beavers. 

Benches offer rest stops where you can let the sweet sounds of catbirds, American redstarts and yellow warblers carry you away. At Taconic State Park, cool off with a swim in a pond or hike to a waterfall. Download the HVRT app to see trail conditions, a map with bathrooms and parking, and a plant guide. Metro-North will take you as far as Wassaic, about 11 miles south of Millerton.

5. MAINE
Acadia Carriage Road Loop From Jordan Pond House
John D. Rockefeller Jr. created a 45-mile network of carriage roads in Acadia National Park to give visitors a peaceful way to explore Mount Desert Island.

This 13.5-mile gravel loop in Acadia National Park follows a trail created by the philanthropist John D. Rockefeller Jr. as part of a 45-mile network of carriage roads to give visitors to Mount Desert Island peaceful motor-free byways. 

Start from the Jordan Pond House, and soon you’ll be climbing next to the pond (most of the route’s 1,000 feet of total climbing is front-loaded), over hand-hewn stone bridges and alongside waterfalls. Much of the rest of the ride winds among dense forests and lakes (at times so close you can see a snapping turtle’s nose rising above the crystal water). 

End back at the Jordan Pond House for its famous popovers, a blueberry lemonade and views of the Bubbles, the park’s iconic twin peaks, bathed in light worthy of a landscape painting. Riders can take the free Bicycle Express shuttle (no e-bikes) from Bar Harbor to the Eagle Lake Carriage Road Trail entrance and start there.

Next up... UNC +3 (0.5u +105 Bovada) - I'd recommend in general take the +3.5 if you can at under -110, but I was closer to thinking ML and wanted to just add 3 pts to not go too out there. 

I may be totally off, but this feels like a game where one team blows the spread out of the water. Either UNC dominates all day and the Clemson demise narrative gets even worse for Dabo, or things go their way and UNC trips over themselves and Dabo buys himself some time. 

However, I just don't see where Clemson can turn it around. 

Chad Morris. Enough said really there. Chad Morris is probably the worst hire any team made on their staff this year. It was said about him during his HC stint back at Arkansas, "The man wakes up and pisses failure." A quintessential retread hire that is able to bounce around. 

His offense is currently 3/27 on 3rd downs (11% conversion). 136th nationally. But the worst part... they have not converted a SINGLE 3rd down on the ground. There is very very little in this run game and OL to help a backup QB settle in. 

They do not have a single OL from the portal. Position coaches, including the OL coach here, had several portal requests denied for the school to offer the players to come to Clemson. Dabo's inability to adapt to the portal is staggering. 

Defensively, they are blitzing at a very very high rate so far this year, but generating very low pressure rate. That is about the worst thing you can do as a defense. Blitzs that don't get home equal big plays for the offense. 

Now UNC could come out and lay a total egg and turn it over and have several STs points given up. But this really isn't so much about UNC, it is that there doesn't seem to be any way for Clemson to turn this around, because this isn't a blip on the radar or some things that need to be tweaked. 

This is a long slow slide that has been coming for years and so many of Dabo's issues running this program in the age of the portal/NIL and favoritism/comfortability in coaching hire decisions was always going to produce this. You can't refuse to adapt in your field of work, only make safe hires, and live on the expectation that past success will somehow naturally lead to future success.

text:
A Stanford convex-optimization lecture offers a bounded lesson for fractional Kelly. It will not estimate your edge; it shows how budgets, return floors, and position limits can turn model uncertainty into a sizing problem.

Start from the balance sheet, not the formula.

Boyd describes a portfolio problem as follows: choose holdings, satisfy the budget, clear a minimum expected-return threshold, obey position and leverage limits, then find the feasible portfolio with the lowest modeled risk.

That order changes how fractional Kelly is used. The theoretical fraction becomes a candidate, not a command. Risk capacity is translated into constraints before any allocation receives capital.

If probability or payoff estimates are optimistic, a position cap contains concentration. If correlations are understated, a leverage limit can reduce amplification. If liquidity assumptions fail, smaller exposure can preserve room to act.

Constraints cannot make uncertain inputs true, and variance cannot capture every risk. They can define an admissible region where one model error is less able to dictate the whole portfolio.

The clip clarifies budgets, return requirements, investment limits, leverage, and modeled risk. It neither derives Kelly nor tells anyone what fraction to use. The payoff is a bounded decision rule: define limits first, optimize second.

At a time when Russia is relentlessly pounding Kyiv, Odesa, and numerous Ukrainian cities, destroying ammunition dumps, fuel depots, and a series of critical logistics hubs, many Ukrainian lawmakers argue that during their recent visit, American negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner conveyed a message of surrender to President Volodymyr Zelensky. In fact, Ukrainian MPs are speaking of "terms of capitulation," implying that the American side asked Kyiv to recognize the territories seized by Russian forces as Russian, and furthermore, to include a corresponding provision in the Constitution of Ukraine. These claims have certainly not been confirmed by either Kyiv or Moscow, while Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov recently characterized related statements as mere speculation. And while Ukrainians see the end of the war approaching through capitulation, figures in Russia emphasize that there is no reason to rush, as the Russian military continues its battlefield advances. Causing particular astonishment is a report by the British newspaper The Telegraph, which claims that British SAS special forces veterans trained Russians for the war against Ukraine.

Terms of surrender

In Ukraine, reports surfaced that special envoys of Donald Trump, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, may have delivered "terms of capitulation" to Kyiv. This statement was made by Verkhovna Rada MP Dmytro Mikisha. His colleague, Anna Skorokhod, had also previously claimed that the American negotiators proposed harsher terms for a peace deal compared to those previously discussed.

Capitulation

The special envoys of the US President, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, may have delivered "terms of capitulation" to Ukraine. This was stated by Verkhovna Rada MP Dmytro Mikisha during an appearance on the YouTube channel "Superposition." "All points pertaining to capitulation re-emerged. What they presented cannot be characterized otherwise. And this coincided in time, in a very distinct manner, with the arrival of Kushner and Witkoff in Ukraine. Consequently, we can assume that these specific gentlemen presented precisely these points," the Ukrainian lawmaker stated. Following these developments, the politician questioned what subjects Kyiv could possibly discuss with Washington moving forward.22_111.jpg

Recognition of territories... as Russian

Mikisha is not the first to make such statements. Earlier, MP Anna Skorokhod stated that Trump's representatives in Kyiv had proposed more disadvantageous terms for a peace agreement compared to those previously debated. According to her, Ukraine was initially not required to recognize the lost territories as Russian. However, Moscow now allegedly considers it necessary to embed this condition into the country's constitutional framework. "There are still certain details that I do not wish to make public, as the information was acquired informally," Skorokhod added.

Tired of fighting

US President Donald Trump also spoke regarding the settlement of the conflict. He did not comment on the outcome of his representatives' visits to Moscow and Kyiv, but he revealed what he considers the primary issue at the present stage. "The delay is caused by two people who hate each other... I know about deals, and these two people are simply tired of fighting," the head of the White House stated, referring to the presidents of Russia and Ukraine, Vladimir Putin and Volodymyr Zelensky. Trump also spoke about his communication with the Russian leader and left open the possibility of holding a personal meeting with Putin in the future. The White House chief did not rule out the prospect of trilateral negotiations.21_91.jpg

What do they say in Russia?

The deputy chairman of the State Duma Committee on International Affairs, Alexey Chepa, stated in a conversation with https://t.co/CH71K9zAtM that such contacts could take place in Abu Dhabi in the coming months, by the end of 2026. "I think everything here depends on the activity shown by those directing Zelensky — the European leaders, who were also present at the meeting in Kyiv. They are trying to push their own agenda. We are ready for trilateral talks," the lawmaker noted.

Positive points

In general, within Russia, the outcomes of the recent visit by American negotiators to Moscow and Kyiv are evaluated more positively than in Ukraine. The first deputy chairwoman of the State Duma Committee on International Affairs, Svetlana Zhurova, emphasized that the Russian and American sides are currently "on the path" toward resolving the conflict. "There are, of course, positive elements. Trump is trying to exert pressure on Ukraine. There are talks taking place at such a high level. We have a complete picture of how we should act and what we need for the definitive resolution of this geopolitical conflict," Zhurova highlighted.

Relying on our own forces

For his part, the advisor to the President of Russia, Nikolai Patrushev, pointed out that Washington can indeed influence the settlement of the conflict; however, according to him, it is hindered by European leadership, which "has no interest in peace whatsoever." Furthermore, the United States is also hampered by its internal contradictions. For this reason, according to Patrushev, Russia has no choice but "to rely solely on its own forces."34_41.jpg

Seeking a compromise

Russia's corresponding, but far stronger, response to Volodymyr Zelensky's 40-day campaign forced Kyiv to seek a compromise. However, Moscow does not need one at this time, points out Russian war correspondent Alexander Kots, who emphasizes that the situation for Ukraine is deteriorating daily, while the Ukrainian armed forces are incapable of inflicting damage of equivalent scale on Russia. "Zelensky suddenly started talking about some sort of compromise. Just in June, he was threatening Russia with a 40-day operation to force peace, and suddenly he lowered his tone. He says Ukraine is ready to seek a compromise with Russia regarding strikes on energy infrastructure and grain exports. We never proposed any compromise either on energy or on grain exports," Kots notes.

Russia cut Ukraine off from the sea

He adds that compromises should be pursued by parties when both have reached a dead end and neither can gain an advantage over the other. However, according to him, no such strategic parity exists between Russia and Ukraine. Elaborating on his thought, he notes that Russia has cut Ukraine off from the sea, depriving it of revenue from grain exports and mineral shipments. In addition, Russian troops are daily striking energy infrastructure, supply networks, and facilities of the Ukrainian military-industrial complex. Meanwhile, the heating season is also approaching. "It is clear that the adversary retaliates, but they are unable to inflict equivalent damage on us. That is why Zelensky is now forced to ask for a compromise. In my view, we need absolutely no compromise right now; it does not correspond to the historical context," the war correspondent emphasizes.444444_12.jpg

The Telegraph: SAS special forces veterans train Russians for the war in Ukraine

Veterans of the British armed forces' special unit, the SAS, are training Russians in conducting military operations in Ukraine, reports British newspaper The Telegraph, citing an internal intelligence memo. The report notes that Western military veterans were recruited to train both Russian civilians and active-duty military personnel. The Telegraph obtained a copy of a memorandum prepared for the Australian Secret Intelligence Service (ASIS), based on interviews with two former members of the Australian special forces and one active reservist. They claim they were offered employment as instructors at training camps in Bulgaria and Serbia, where Russian clients were allegedly present.

Training in northern Bulgaria

The memorandum states that at the camp in Medzheni, northern Bulgaria, which is operated by the military training company Alfa-Metal, instructors from diverse professional backgrounds are employed, including veterans from the SAS, the Australian Commando Regiment, US law enforcement, and the US Navy SEALs. At the same time, it is highlighted that the Alfa-Metal center offers special forces courses and advanced sniper training, costing approximately 4,000 euros per person. The programs target potential employees of private military companies, bodyguards, and corporate security personnel. However, the intelligence note mentions that since 2022, when Moscow launched its military operation in Ukraine, private training camps in Europe continue to accept Russian citizens into training modules, including advanced hand-to-hand combat. Special forces veterans interviewed during information gathering about the camp stated that current employees told them the center continued to train Russian citizens up until 2025, the newspaper claims. The Telegraph notes, however, that Alfa-Metal itself denied training Russian citizens at the training camps owned by the company.444333.png

Economist: Only 2 options remain for Ukrainians

With stockpiles of PAC-3 interceptors for Patriot air defense systems nearly depleted, Kyiv now has only two courses of action remaining, the Economist points out. The report notes that the situation for Ukraine is complicated by jet-powered Russian unmanned aerial vehicles, ballistic missiles—production of which has increased to 100 units per month—as well as the shortage of interceptor missiles for Patriot systems. Meanwhile, the Freja missile defense system is not yet ready for operational deployment and may acquire some operational capability only by 2028. "At this moment, Ukraine is left with only two options. The first is to reinforce and conceal infrastructure and industrial facilities while securing an adequate supply of spare parts. The second is the so-called 'left-of-launch' strategy, which aims to reduce the number of missiles available to Russia," stresses the Economist. The publication notes that Ukrainian forces could target missile launchers. However, this is a difficult task, and even the United States, in the war in Iran, faces difficulties destroying mobile launchers, journalists highlighted. For this reason, Matthew Bint from the International Institute for Strategic Studies called on Kyiv to turn its attention to Russian missile manufacturing factories and attempt to strike them.

The Interview … Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor Say the End of the World Is Now on the Table

NYT Gift Article link
12SEP2026
By David Marchese
https://t.co/wFVftj1YSz
The current political stakes, as Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor see them, could not be higher. 

In the view of these two influential leftist thinkers, a driving motivation behind far-right politics at the moment is nothing less than the apocalypse. 

In their alarming new book, “End Times Fascism and the Fight for the Living World,” Klein, the author of the best sellers “The Shock Doctrine” and “Doppelganger,” and Taylor, an author and documentarian as well as a founder of the Debt Collective, a debtors’ union, argue that a powerful coalition of religious fundamentalists, ethnonationalists and tech oligarchs (Elon Musk chief among them) is actively — and successfully — hastening the destruction of the world as we know it. 

Why? 

Because they believe that they’re primed to thrive on the other side of catastrophe, everyone else be damned. 

This is a sobering, scary vision of contemporary political battles. 

But as the still hopeful Klein and Taylor explain, they wrote their book because they believe the conclusion is far from foregone.

Video

Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor Say the End of the World Is Now on the Table

In their new book, “End Times Fascism and the Fight for the Living World,” Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor argue that fundamentalists, ethnonationalists and tech oligarchs are hastening the destruction of the world as we know it.

Just to start: What is “end-times fascism?”

Naomi Klein: End-times fascism is a fascism that is very much in conversation with planetary-scale existential crises; a fascism that is taking the end of this world for granted. We thought long and hard about the politics of putting any kind of qualifier on a word like “fascism.” And the reason we ended up deciding that it did need that is we thought about how our world has changed since Mussolini declared himself a fascist. Our fascists have weapons that last century’s fascists couldn’t dream of. There was no atomic bomb. Hitler and Mussolini died before the Trinity test. They didn’t understand that fossil fuels were warming the planet. Our world has become more dangerous, and fascism has changed in response and has made peace with the idea of collapse. And now what they’re fighting for is who is going to survive that cataclysm.

How does end-times fascism make itself felt in the world today?

Klein: The first thing I thought of was the SpaceX I.P.O. I think what resonates is like: Hey, don’t the billionaires have bunkers now? Aren’t they somehow prepping? What is this sort of fixation on leaving the Earth behind? What is he saving humanity from exactly? Why do we accept that this world needs escape from?

Astra Taylor: It’s not a dominant political worldview, even on the right, but it is a term we think applies to some of the most powerful people in the world who are leading governments and companies. Those are the evangelical Christian Zionists, who are a very potent political force in the United States; that’s Zionists in Israel. These are real groups of people with real power. Then there are the tech end-timers, who believe that it’s worth incinerating this world as long as they can build their virtual one and that we are inevitably heading toward some sort of digital superintelligence, some singularity. And then the third group are the ethnonationalists, who believe that the nation is under existential threat from immigration, from cultural change, and their response is to fortress the nation, to cast out the domestic enemies. These groups are different. There are contradictions, they’re messy and not totally coherent, but they’re responding to this sense that the world is increasingly fraught and dangerous — which it is — and they’re responding by shutting down and trying to defend their group. And they’ve made this very dangerous alliance.

Klein: I would say that effort is embodied by the Trump administration. The massive funding coming from Silicon Valley, and Elon Musk in particular. What exactly is going on? The first time Trump was president, many of these same billionaires were criticizing him. They were upset when he left the Paris climate accord. Zuckerberg was condemning him. Bezos was launching an Earth prize. They were positioning themselves as the people who were going to save the planet. I want to ask an Elon Musk question. He is a defining character of our age, for better or worse. I think, for people who like him, there’s a real grandeur to the idea of SpaceX rockets and colonizing outer space. We’re dealing with trillionaires; that wealth has merged with the most powerful military in the world. But also, Wow, you get to ride a subway and who knows what will happen, and it will take you to some amazing place where you can eat something you can’t make at home. Or just any of the psychedelia of this part of the natural world: On the very, very dark nights, the water is completely bioluminescent, and you look at your own limbs and they’re made of pure light — no mushrooms required! It is a tragedy for them, and an existential crisis for us, that the people who are closest to the levers of power on this planet are not enraptured by the beauty that is already here and all around us.

That’s a funky statistic, though. It’s very dependent on how a given Christian interprets “end times.” A Catholic might believe that we’ve been in the end times since Jesus ascended. So half of Christians believing in end times is not necessarily the same as meaning they want to ——

Klein: Accelerate it, yeah. But I just don’t think that these are marginal ideas. These are some of the most powerful stories in our culture. They’re incredibly deeply encoded. Whether we’re religious or not, they’re in us, and there’s a kind of drive to repeat them because the stories are so powerful. So we need mythic stories of our own. It can’t just be, We need universal health care, and we need affordable lives. We also need myth. We need to recover a sense of wonder and awe at this world. That’s why it’s worth looking at it. There’s things that we can learn from what is resonating.

Why does it seem like the left has not been able to harness apocalyptic energy in the way the right has?

Taylor: I think building multiracial democracy is harder than building fascism or authoritarianism. Because we don’t want to just grab the levers of power. You want to share power, and you have to figure out how to live together. So I think our project is just inherently more difficult.

Klein: In answer to your question, as somebody who’s been on the left for a long time, we’ve gotten closer than at any other point. For those of us who were part of the Bernie Sanders campaign — I was living in the U.S. at the time and was part of that campaign as a surrogate for his Green New Deal program, which I felt was the kind of response that both addressed emissions and people’s economic needs. But in politics you don’t get a prize for second place. I do think that this wave that Mamdani has helped lead, and this wave of D.S.A. candidates who are winning in the primaries, speaks to the fact that the left is a lot more serious about fighting fascism; the willingness to call it fascism, to call it genocide, to use the words that describe reality are actually far better at fighting fascism than a supposedly safe centrism that is collapsing around the world.

Where do you see opportunities on the right for pushback against end-times fascists?

Klein: The most awkward alliance is around the big tech companies and the MAGA base. They don’t like the idea of being tracked by their phones, so there are definitely opportunities there. We are seeing it in these local meetings, which is really interesting to me, having done this research around the anti-vaccine, anti-masking, anti-Covid health-measures movement during Covid, which then rolls into a movement for book banning and anti-trans rights. Those were the issues that were making people storm city hall and go to a town hall meeting. Today the thing that is bringing people into their town hall meetings is opposition to the data center down the road.

Taylor: We talk about data centers being icons of this futurelessness. There used to be a kind of bargain: You’d get a factory in the town and that meant there was some pollution and maybe some tax abatements, but there were also jobs that supported your family, even if the wages weren’t the best. And going to Memphis, for example, where Elon Musk now has three supercomputers, and meeting the people there who are fighting against this development because Musk is powering them with gas turbines. Some of them are as big as 30 football fields. And there are basically no jobs. What is the offer?

Are there signs, little flares on the horizon, that would give you clues that the influence of end-times fascists is receding?

Taylor: Minneapolis is a great example. I think that the Trump administration went into that assault thinking that it would be greeted gleefully, at least by its base, and that people would thrill at the video being circulated, celebrating the violence, and actually they overreached. They shot people in the street, and even some of their base were appalled by that. So I think we’re seeing signs that they’re definitely not infallible. Ultimately what we would like to see is some of these people being held accountable. And this goes to the attacks on the I.C.C. [International Criminal Court] and this constant assertion, “Well, we have immunity,” right?

Klein: That’s why it matters when Mamdani says that Netanyahu belongs in The Hague and he should be arrested. For too long we have not put forward our own vision for accountability, a serious one, using these institutions. What would it mean to really hold war criminals accountable and have it apply across the board, not only to people in Africa who commit crimes, or the Philippines, but also the United States and Israel? It would be the beginning of addressing such deep disillusionment, because we are up against a very widespread feeling that there’s nothing you can do. Doing a few things starts to break that spell.

What you just said — could American politicians be held accountable by the I.C.C.? — my first thought is, That’ll never happen. I’m not saying it should or shouldn’t happen. It just seems unlikely.

Taylor: Sometimes things that seem improbable happen because people organize to make them so.

Klein: We didn’t write the book because we think these people are fascinating. We wrote this book because we want people to fight them and beat them. We use this word that neither Astra nor I have ever used before because we’re not nationalist people: We call them “traitors.” Not traitors to a nation, not traitors to a flag or a border, but traitors to creation, traitors to life. And we spent a lot of time looking at where this project is weak. Where it’s strong is money, weapons. We’re dealing with trillionaires; that wealth has merged with the most powerful military in the world. I’m not nostalgic for the last century’s fascists, let’s be clear about that, but they had an offer to their base. They’re like, Let us steal the homes of the Jews and the Slavs and live happily ever after in your Lebensraum Ukraine. The people we’re calling end-times fascists don’t have an offer to their base beyond sadism.

One of the through lines of your book is that end-times fascists are not seeing the beauty of the world and the things that truly make life worthwhile. What are the things that you think, Oh, if only they could see what I see.

Taylor: A big one, and it’s a classic fascist trope, is the fear of the city, the fear of encountering people from different walks of life. We write about how powerful the Mamdani campaign was in re-enchanting the city — not romanticizing it, not saying it’s perfect. Yes, the subways have problems. But also, Wow, you get to ride a subway and who knows what will happen, and it will take you to some amazing place where you can eat something you can’t make at home. Just encountering and not fearing diversity but reveling in it. And absolutely the more-than-human world. Naomi lives somewhere with really good nature, so I feel like she has to take that one.

Klein: Oh, my god, where to start? I live in British Columbia. Honestly I feel the most sadness and rage at a willingness to let it all burn, or to try to escape when I see a dorsal fin of an orca slice through the waters of the Salish Sea, where I’m fortunate enough to live. Or just any of the psychedelia of this part of the natural world: On the very, very dark nights, the water is completely bioluminescent, and you look at your own limbs and they’re made of pure light — no mushrooms required! It is a tragedy for them, and an existential crisis for us, that the people who are closest to the levers of power on this planet are not enraptured by the beauty that is already here and all around us.
