text:
What Democracy Is For
A response to International IDEA’s Global State of Democracy 2026: Democracy in an Age of Conflict

International IDEA’s Global State of Democracy 2026: Democracy in an Age of Conflict examines a disturbing conjunction: democratic institutions are weakening in many countries at the same time as violent conflict is becoming more common.

In a functioning democracy, losing political power must not mean losing your place in society.

A person can lose an election and still have a future in the country. An organisation can fail in its political aims and continue to organise, criticise the government and argue for another course. A proposal can be defeated in parliament without those who supported it losing the right to say that the decision was wrong.

Political defeat must not become the destruction of a person’s future.

That may sound obvious in a stable democracy. But much of the IDEA report is about what happens when it stops being obvious, when courts, rights, political competition or the ability to organise can no longer be relied upon after power changes hands.

An independent court matters when somebody needs protection from an arbitrary decision. Freedom of expression matters when those in power would prefer a problem to remain unspoken. The right to organise matters because people acting together can challenge conditions they could never change alone.

International IDEA uses a much broader understanding of democracy than elections alone. Its framework covers representation, rights, the rule of law and participation. Elections sit alongside effective parliaments, independent courts, access to justice, a free press and room for civil society to operate.

The figures show more stagnation than collapse, alongside significant declines in a substantial number of countries. Between 2020 and 2025, 81 per cent of the country-level measures showed no statistically significant change. Yet 98 countries, 57 per cent of those assessed, deteriorated significantly in at least one democratic factor, while 55, 32 per cent, improved in at least one. IDEA excludes Basic Welfare from this comparison because much of the apparent improvement reflected recovery in life expectancy after the Covid-19 pandemic.

Freedom of expression and freedom of the press were among the areas with the widest deterioration.

So the picture is not one of democracy disappearing everywhere. Much of the world is stagnating, often at levels that are already unsatisfactory, while important democratic protections are weakening.

There is another reason to pay attention. Uppsala Conflict Data Program figures cited by IDEA record 65 state-based conflicts in 2025, almost twice the number in 2010 and the highest total in a single year since the series began in 1946. That is not a small fluctuation. There were more state-based conflicts in 2025 than in any other year covered by the post-war data.

This is the background to IDEA’s examination of the connection between democracy and conflict. But should human beings have to demonstrate that freedom prevents war before they are entitled to freedom? The ability to speak without intimidation, seek justice and live without arbitrary persecution is already part of a decent society.

When political defeat becomes dangerous
In a functioning democracy, losing an election does not normally mean losing your ability to influence what happens next. There will be another election. A court may overturn an unlawful decision. Organisations can continue campaigning. Newspapers can investigate the government. People can persuade others and attempt to build a majority for another course.

Looking at the world today, it is not difficult to find systems in which losing may bring imprisonment, dispossession, suppression of an organisation or permanent exclusion from political life. A community may reasonably fear that the rights which allowed it to participate will disappear once its opponents take power.

That is not just a harsher kind of defeat. It changes what is at stake. If losing means prison, exile, loss of livelihood or the destruction of your organisation, then accepting the result may also mean accepting that there is no peaceful way back. In that situation, it is not difficult to understand why some people stop believing that ordinary politics can protect them.

When political losses can be reversed through credible procedures, opponents have reasons to remain within those procedures. Elections provide another opportunity to win support. Courts and enforceable rights make it possible to challenge an injustice without first having to remove the government.

But institutions cannot provide that security simply by existing on paper. People must believe they will still work when the dispute becomes serious.

There is a simple test here for anyone who says they believe in democracy. It is easy to defend judicial independence when a court rules against our opponents, or press freedom when journalists expose people we dislike. The real test comes when the judgement goes against us.

The point is that these protections have to apply even when they are inconvenient.

International IDEA also gives considerable attention to countries between established democracy and established autocracy. These hybrid systems may permit elections while offering little genuine competition or weak protection for those who lose. The report argues that such conditions are associated with greater conflict risk.

One explanation is that an authoritarian state can suppress organised opposition, often brutally, while a functioning democracy offers alternative ways of pursuing grievances. A weak system between the two may permit mobilisation while lacking institutions capable of settling the disputes that follow.

But this is not a universal formula. “Hybrid regime” can cover very different situations: weak public institutions, difficult political transitions, excluded communities, contested sovereignty or divided control over armed forces.

State capacity therefore matters as well. Courts must be able to enforce their decisions. Public institutions have to function throughout the territory. A constitution cannot do much to protect people if armed groups control parts of the country and the government cannot enforce its decisions there.

Myanmar and Sudan show what this can look like in practice. Myanmar’s 2021 coup occurred in a country where the military had never been fully brought under civilian authority and where longstanding armed conflicts already existed. Sudan’s civilian transition similarly took place alongside rival armed organisations with enormous independent power.

In both countries, democracy broke down, but that does not by itself explain the violence.

Nor does this mean that we should simply prefer a stronger state. A state strong enough to impose its will but too unaccountable to be challenged presents another danger. Public institutions need enough capacity to govern while remaining under effective public control.

The majority must be able to govern, but the minority must remain part of society, with rights and a future.

According to the report, established democracies very rarely fight serious wars against one another.

That does not mean democratic countries are peaceful by nature. Democracies have fought many wars against non-democratic states and have repeatedly intervened militarily abroad. IDEA itself stresses this limitation. The democratic-peace finding applies to pairs of democratic countries, not to the behaviour of democracies in general.

The explanation is still disputed, but the relationship itself is remarkably strong. And IDEA’s next finding is difficult to dismiss: in 2015, 42.6 per cent of relationships between states were between two countries that met at least a minimal democratic threshold. By 2025 that had fallen to 34.4 per cent. That is a substantial change in only ten years. A significant part of the international system has moved out of the category in which serious war has historically been exceptionally rare.

How far does the evidence take us?
One thing I appreciate about the IDEA report is that much of its academic discussion is careful.

It explicitly says that the simultaneous rise in conflict and democratic decline does not prove that one caused the other. Many recent conflicts multiplied in countries and regions already affected by violence.

The policy recommendations sometimes go further.

Suppose a study finds an association between a particular institution and a particular kind of violence. Later that becomes evidence that the institution prevents conflict, and then a recommendation to fund that institution as a means of preventing war.

Perhaps the recommendation is sound. But something has changed at each step.

Was causation actually demonstrated? Did the study concern interstate war, civil conflict or something narrower? Does the policy recommendation contain an additional judgement that the original study never tested? And even if funding is justified in general, does the research tell us which countries, organisations or programmes should receive it, and under what conditions it is likely to work?

There need be no dishonesty in this. Governments cannot wait for complete certainty before acting. But public money can still be spent in places where it achieves very little.

Citizens should be able to see where evidence ends and judgement begins.

Good intentions do not remove the need for evidence.

Civil society provides one example. IDEA places considerable weight on research about social accountability and argues in its recommendations that active civil society reduces conflict risk and contributes to positive peace.

There is real research behind this, but some of the evidence concerns serious disputes between countries. It is understandable that IDEA applies the finding more broadly, but the original study does not establish the same relationship for every form of political violence.

Civil society is also not uniformly beneficial. Organisations can expose corruption, bring communities together and provide peaceful ways of acting collectively. They can also mobilise people against those of a different religion, ethnicity or nationality.

What people organise for matters.

Democracy assistance raises a similar issue. There is credible evidence that such assistance can modestly improve democratic institutions and practices. IDEA then argues that democracy support should be treated as part of national-security strategy, partly because prevention is cheaper than military action after conflict begins.

There is a plausible case for that policy. But evidence that democracy aid improves some democratic outcomes, together with evidence that preventing wars saves money, does not tell us how many wars democracy assistance actually prevents.

That does not make the recommendation wrong. It means part of the argument remains an inference.

If the research is uncertain, the policy argument should say so.

Why the United States matters beyond the United States
International IDEA gives considerable attention to the United States.

It identifies seven significant declines across factors and subfactors between 2020 and 2025, involving access to justice, economic equality, parliamentary effectiveness, freedom of expression, freedom of the press, freedom for political parties and judicial independence. Several of these trends began before the present administration.

The report’s comparable index data run through 2025. Its discussion of events during 2026 is more qualitative. Both matter, but they are different kinds of evidence.

Democratic deterioration in any country is first a problem for the people living there. But the United States possesses exceptional military, economic and diplomatic power. Decisions made there affect wars, alliances, development assistance, international institutions and international law.

Millions of people affected by those decisions have no vote in American elections.

Their lives are not less important for that reason.

This is why the condition of American democracy is legitimately a matter of concern far beyond the United States.

A question the report leaves me with
One of the strengths of the IDEA report is that it takes democracy well beyond the ballot box.

But that leaves me with a further question.

If democracy is concerned with how power is distributed and constrained, what should we make of economic power?

We pay close attention to who sits in parliament, whether judges are independent and whether elections are fair. We ask much less often who controls investment, credit, workplaces, land, large corporations or media organisations.

International IDEA includes economic equality in its framework, which is important. But income inequality, wealth inequality and inequality of economic decision-making power are not the same thing.

A society can redistribute income while control of investment and workplaces remains highly concentrated.

Research from the United States has found substantially stronger relationships between policy outcomes and the preferences of affluent citizens and organised business interests than between policy and the preferences of average citizens. This does not mean political inequality simply rises with income inequality. Institutions affect how easily economic resources become political power.

This is no longer only an abstract question about the relationship between wealth and influence. Billionaires can now combine enormous financial resources with ownership of newspapers, social-media platforms and other forms of communication, while also funding political campaigns and gaining direct access to governments. Elon Musk’s interventions in European politics are one obvious example, but he is hardly alone. Jeff Bezos owns the Washington Post, Mark Zuckerberg controls Meta’s global platforms, and billionaire money has become increasingly important in American elections. These people do not all support the same politics, and wealth does not guarantee that they get what they want. But their ability to influence political debate, political organisations and sometimes the conditions under which public debate takes place is on a completely different scale from that of an ordinary citizen. Reuters documented Musk’s direct support for Germany’s AfD during the 2025 election campaign and Bezos’s ownership role at the Washington Post, while the Brennan Center has documented the growing role of megadonors and record levels of outside political spending in the 2024 US election.

A democracy should at least ask what that does to the idea of equal political influence.

So who decides where investment goes? Who makes the important decisions in a workplace? What influence do the people affected have?

These are democratic questions too.

The research on economic democracy remains limited. Union membership is associated with greater political participation, and some studies link stronger workplace representation with more equal political responsiveness and greater political engagement. But this does not establish that cooperatives, unions or workplace democracy prevent democratic collapse or war.

A preference for a particular economic arrangement does not justify claiming more for it than the evidence supports.

At the same time, the moral case for giving people meaningful influence over their working lives does not have to wait for proof that it prevents war.

People spend a large part of their lives working under arrangements that affect their security and opportunities. Whether they have a meaningful voice in those arrangements is itself a question of dignity and power.

What democracy is for
Reading the IDEA report ultimately brings me back to what democracy is for. For all its weaknesses, I think democracy is the best political arrangement humanity has developed so far. The question is not whether we should abandon it, but how much further we can take the democratic principle.

People will disagree about laws, resources, beliefs and the direction of society. No political arrangement can ensure that everyone gets what they want. What democracy can do is make disagreement less dangerous.

It allows people to lose an election without losing their place in society. It protects unpopular opinions. It gives people peaceful ways to challenge decisions and makes public power answerable to those who live under it.

Political democracy gives people a voice over public power. Economic democracy asks whether people should also have a meaningful voice over economic powers that shape so much of their lives.

I see that as an extension of democracy, not an alternative to it. We already accept that political power should not simply be concentrated in a few hands without accountability. It seems reasonable to ask the same question about economic power, particularly when wealth, ownership and control can also become political influence.

None of this guarantees a good society. Institutions can fail. Majorities can behave badly. Civil society can become exclusionary. Economic democracy can be badly designed. Democratic governments can wage unjust wars.

But some things should not depend on who happens to win.

The opportunity to learn, to work, to seek justice and to live without persecution cannot be distributed as the reward of political victory.

A child’s need for food does not begin when the parents’ party wins an election, and it does not disappear when that party loses.

People should be free to disagree about how society can best provide these things. They should be able to criticise one another’s proposals, expose failures and try something different.

But nobody’s claim to a dignified existence should depend upon winning that argument.

The ballot box can help decide who will govern for a time.

It cannot decide whose humanity is to be respected.

References

Davies, Shawn, Therése Pettersson and Magnus Öberg. 2026. “Organized Violence 1989–2025, and Violent Political Protests.” Journal of Peace Research, 63(4).

text:
The Fundamentals
The primary driver in this matchup is a massive starting pitching advantage for Philadelphia. Cristopher Sánchez brings an elite profile to the mound, carrying a 2.79 ERA, a 1.21 WHIP, and 210 strikeouts over 187.1 innings. On the other side, the Nationals are rolling out rookie Jackson Kent, who is struggling heavily with traffic, posting a 6.59 ERA and a massive 1.83 WHIP in his limited action. 

While the weather features a 7 mph wind blowing out to left field—which generally favors offense—this dynamic disproportionately hurts the pitcher who puts more runners on base. Kent's 1.83 WHIP means he is constantly pitching out of the stretch with traffic, making him highly vulnerable to a blow-up inning in run-friendly conditions. 

My Probability
Given the severe discrepancy in starting pitching stability and WHIP, I make the Phillies winning this game about a 68% probability. 

The Value & Best Execution
Polymarket: Phillies 67¢ (67% implied)
Sportsbook: Phillies -217 (68.4% break-even)

With my read at 68% and the market sitting around 67-68%, this game is priced accurately and there is no significant edge here. The steep price reflects the obvious pitching mismatch. If you do want to back Philadelphia, Polymarket's 67¢ offers slightly better execution than laying the heavy -217 moneyline at the traditional sportsbook. 

*(Note: I was unable to isolate a Kalshi moneyline market for tonight's specific game).*

Texas State Rep. Venton Jones Apologizes to Women After Jasmine Crockett’s Chris Brown Honor Sparks Backlash

Texas State Rep. Venton Jones is addressing the backlash surrounding Congresswoman Jasmine Crockett’s appearance with Chris Brown and Usher during their recent concert at AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas—and he’s starting with an apology.

During an interview with Don Lemon, Jones apologized to  women and anyone who has experienced DV, saying it was never his intention to “stoke the traumas” connected to domestic violence.

“I want to offer an apology,” Jones said.

The comments come after Jones and Crockett appeared onstage during the September 12 concert. Crockett presented Brown and Usher with formal recognitions, creating a moment that quickly spread across social media and sparked a wave of criticism.

The backlash centered largely on Brown’s history, particularly his 2009 assault case involving Rihanna. Brown has also faced other legal issues over the years and recently pleaded guilty in the United Kingdom to an affray charge stemming from a 2023 nightclub incident.

Was Jasmine Crockett wrong?

text:
Who is Nick Blankenburg?
Position: Defenceman (RHD) Height: 5-foot-9 Weight: 177 Pounds 2025-26 Season: 61 GP, 24 points, 59 blocks, minus-10, 16:48 TOI

An undrafted free agent signed by the Blue Jackets out of Michigan, Blankenburg spent four years in the NCAA where he amassed 68 points in 133 games, while also captaining the Wolverines in his final season.

His NHL debut season went pretty great as well, and though he only appeared in seven games - he did have three points. His best singular NHL season was in 2024-25 where he added 16 points in 60 games, with only a minus-two in a career-high 19:33 TOI. 

Nashville clearly liked what they saw, and gave him as much room to run as possible.
He's a much more physical guy than his size would dictate, and while he won't blow you away offensively, he does offer much more upside in that aspect than Troy Stecher and Myers, and could fight with Emil Andrae as part of that third-pairing. Also being a right-handed shot, that gives head coach Jim Hiller another versatile option to plug in.

What Nick Blankenburg needs to do to earn a spot with the Maple Leafs

Honestly, he doesn't need to do much except do what he did the last two seasons. He has better stats and underlying numbers than Myers, and with Stecher being 32, Blankenburg offers a younger player with higher upside.

Also with questions about Chris Tanev's status with the team this season, Blankenburg would give the Maple Leafs the perfect replacement in the interim. Oliver Ekman-Larsson can slide to the second pair with Jake McCabe, and he and Andrae can be the dual two-way forces on the third pair.

Blankenburg has to come into camp and outplay not only Myers and Stecher, but also make sure that he doesn't get overshadowed by a prospect like Ben Danford or Vinny Borgesi - of who Blankenburg is similar to is size and style.
It isn't an easy path to the Maple Leafs, but clearly they see enough of something in Blankenburg to invite him to camp. 

It's just up to him to take that opportunity and turn it into an NHL contract.

text:
Running Against a Black Man, Benson Assumes She Has the Black Vote
She thinks demographics are her destiny, and even picked a white running mate

By James Dickson @downi75 

View John James through the eyes of a black parent, and you’ll see why some black voters could find a new home in the Republican Party in 2026.

James is talented and accomplished. His career path took him from West Point to an Apache helicopter to the business world and then into politics.

He left Washington because he thought it was important to fix the state he’ll someday leave to his three sons.

James shows that you can reach the heights, in life and in politics, through hard work. He is the product of a two-parent home, and raises his three boys in a two-parent home.

The James family—he one he was born into, and the one he created with wife Liz—shows what’s possible what comes after you conquer generational curses. You start building legacies.

Jocelyn Benson, the Democrat nominee in the governor’s race, has only abortion, government dependency and a victimhood mentality to offer black people. John James shows what’s behind Door No. 2.

Now, view Jocelyn Benson through the eyes of a black woman.

“What they see is what they’ll be” is the idea undergirding a slogan we’ve all heard plenty of in recent years: “Representation matters.”

Gov. Gretchen Whitmer was shrewd in 2018 when she picked Garlin Gilchrist as her running mate. Whitmer had lost Detroit to Shri Thanedar in the Democrat primary and would not leave anything to chance in the general election. Democrat math does not work without the black vote.

Whitmer chose a black son of suburban Detroit, and showed herself willing to play the game of politics.

Benson, on the other hand, went with a fellow white woman, Sen. Winnie Brinks, as her running mate. Where Whitmer was shrewd, Benson is selfish.

Picking Brinks is Benson applying “representation matters” to her own comfort level, rather than the voters of Michigan. It’s Benson assuming that the electorate is frozen in amber, and that black women will support her no matter what. What else are they going to do? Vote Republican?

Benson’s mentor, Hillary Clinton, could have told her what happens when you fail to balance the ticket. In 2016, Hillary Clinton tapped Tim Kaine was her running mate. After eight years of Obama, Clinton reverted the Democrats back to an all-white ticket. Voters didn’t buy it, and she lost to Donald Trump, including in Michigan, where Trump only won by 10,000 votes.

Republicans give Benson the ick, so she’s assuming—there goes that word again—that black women will feel the same way.

And in a normal year, they might. But not with a man who reminds them of their son on the ballot.

When Barack Obama ran for president in 2008, I supported him even though I was a Republican. (I didn’t like John McCain, then or now.)

I wrote about this in the Detroit News. Here’s what I had to say:

“When conservative friends ask how I can support a standard-issue liberal, I think of my unborn grandchildren. When those kids ask whom I voted for in 2008, I can't imagine telling them that I bypassed what is possibly a once-in-a-lifetime chance to vote for a candidate of African descent.”

I’m a student of history. Back then, I thought it would be cool to have someone who looks like me on the back page of the history book, among the pictures of the presidents.

But the distinction between “African descent” and “black American” was not as clear to me as it should have been.

Barack Obama was not a heritage black American. He was an international arrival with just enough black dust sprinkled on him to qualify for “first.”

The guy’s middle name is Hussein. That should have been my first clue something was not quite right. Only when the second black candidate’s middle name was Devi was it clear to black people that Democrats never route these opportunities to heritage black Americans.

I say that to say this: When presented with a chance to rewrite history, people do things they would not normally do. They vote how they would not normally vote.

“Third woman governor,” as Benson wants to be, does not motivate people. Given that the first two—Jennifer Granholm and Whitmer—brought Lost Decades to Michigan, it’s closer to a demerit.

But “first black governor” still has some currency in a community low on firsts.

And unlike Obama, John James actually is one of us. He changes the permission structure for black voters in a way not seen in decades.

And unlike Wayne County Executive Bill Lucas in 1986, James is running for an open seat, not against a popular incumbent. With two months until Election Day, it’s anybody’s game.

Jocelyn Benson is assuming that old ways, old patterns and old habits will hold in 2026. She is playing a dangerous game.

Jocelyn Benson thinks she has the black vote in the bag. I wouldn’t be so sure about that.

2/2

When members of Congress become this deeply invested in political disputes thousands of miles away from their own districts, start paying attention.

Pay attention to lobbying, political relationships, advocacy organizations, publicly disclosed campaign contributions, congressional travel and meetings, and who continually receives access.

And yes: follow the money.

Please do not insult everyone’s intelligence and pretend these aren’t legitimate questions worth asking.

But again try and be precise; if the interests originate in Albania, say Albania.
If the interests originate from Kosovo, say Kosovo. If the lobbying is for Kosovo, say Kosovo lobby. If the political problem is Kurti, say Kurti.
And it is Kurti.

We can’t afford to be imprecise when discussing these things with our Republican colleagues and friends. First, we come across as confusing. Second, we waste valuable time explaining exactly which actors and institutions we mean. In politics, that lost time matters.

Precision matters when you’re trying to understand how Washington works, and even more when you’re trying to become politically effective here.

Ultimately, Keith Self and Joe Wilson don’t represent Kosovo, Serbia or Albania.

They represent Americans.

That is why what I watched today bothered me.

Bill Keating was sitting there attacking President Trump and his administration’s Balkan policy, and two Republican congressmen sitting right there offered none of the immediate pushback I expected while it was happening.

That’s the criticism.

And when politicians are simultaneously this invested in political questions happening thousands of miles away, Americans have every right to ask who is pushing these positions, whose interests are being advanced and, most importantly, how any of it serves the United States.

Because America First means America First.

Balkan policy should serve American interests before the interests of Belgrade, Pristina, Tirana, Sarajevo or anybody else.

And Serbian Americans have an additional reason to watch particularly closely.

We understand that region. We have roots and families there. We understand the history, mentality and political games in ways the average American understandably has neither the time nor reason to study every day.

That gives us a responsibility to understand what is happening here in Washington, too.

When something doesn’t add up on both fronts, when we believe something works against American interests and Serbian interests simultaneously, we’re going to say something.

If you want to play political games 5,000 miles away and those games influence American foreign policy, Americans have every right to ask why.

And Serbian Americans are going to ask twice.

Being a Republican and sitting quietly while a Democratic congressman attacks your own President right next to you is one thing.

Being deeply invested in questionable policy thousands of miles away while doing it raises another set of questions entirely.

So yes, I’m watching.

And if you’re a Republican and you’ve forgotten which country’s interests come first, don’t be surprised when some of us start using that old four-letter acronym:

RINO.

America First means exactly what it says.

America first.

We’re watching. Closely 🇺🇸🇷🇸

text:
🇷🇺 NO ENERGY TRUCE EXISTS — AND MOSCOW NEVER HID THAT FACT 🇷🇺

Zelensky’s “No” to CBS was not a revelation. It was confirmation. There is no energy truce. There never was a signed halt. Washington floated an idea. Kiev attached conditions that amount to political surrender. Moscow stated the obvious: energy is commerce, sanctions are the real blockade, and tanker safety is not optional. 🛢️

The Ukrainian leader framed it as if Russia sells oil while Ukraine merely “gives people electricity.” That is theatre. Russia’s oil and gas are the backbone of a sovereign economy under siege by Western price caps, seized tankers, and drone campaigns against refineries hundreds of kilometres inside Russian territory. Ukraine’s grid is a wartime target because it powers mobilisation, rail, air defence, and Western-supplied systems. Pretending the two are morally identical is propaganda, not analysis.

🇷🇺 PESKOV SAID WHAT EVERY MARKET ALREADY KNOWS 🇷🇺

Kremlin spokesman Peskov did not reject a pause. He welcomed the idea as “very good” and then named the missing pieces: safe commercial shipping for oil tankers, and the lifting of what Moscow calls unlawful restrictions on energy exports. Without those, a paper truce changes nothing on world markets.

 Diesel prices, shortages, and tanker risk do not vanish because a television clip sounded hopeful.

Ukraine has shown no consistent inclination to guarantee that security. Strikes on refineries, depots, and related infrastructure have continued. Russia’s position is blunt: stop attacking civilian economic infrastructure that feeds global supply, stop threatening the Black Sea and Baltic routes, and stop treating sanctions as a permanent weapon. Only then does “stabilisation” become more than a slogan.

⚡ ENERGY IS NOT CHARITY — IT IS SOVEREIGNTY ⚡

For Russia, energy is not a hobby. It is budget, industry, employment, and leverage that existed long before 2022. Sanctions were designed to collapse that system. They have not. They have rerouted trade, raised costs for Europe, and still left Moscow able to sell. 

Demanding that Russia freeze its energy war while the sanctions architecture stays intact is not de-escalation. It is a one-sided pause that leaves the economic siege in place.

Zelenskyy’s extra demand — that Washington must first “ensure” Russia is ready to end the entire war — turns a limited infrastructure idea into a full political precondition. That is why there is no truce. Kiev wants guarantees of Russian strategic defeat dressed up as a humanitarian energy deal. 

Moscow wants sanctions relief and tanker safety as the price of any real market effect. Those are different starting points.

🇷🇺 THE WEST WANTS CHEAP FUEL WITHOUT PAYING THE POLITICAL BILL 🇷🇺

American politics is staring at midterms and pump prices. Blaming Ukrainian drones for diesel spikes is convenient. Removing the sanctions that restrict Russian product from flowing legally would be more effective — and politically harder. Peskov simply said the quiet part: markets calm when supply is legal, insured, and not hunted at sea.

A genuine energy pause would require reciprocity that Kiev has not offered without total-war conditions attached. Russia will not disarm its economic defence while the other side keeps the right to strike refineries and while Western restrictions stay locked. That is not stubbornness. That is how states that still control their own resources behave.

There is no energy truce because the terms on offer were never equal. 🇷🇺🛢️⚡

🇷🇺🇷🇺 THE REALITY BEHIND ZELENSKYY'S LATEST STORY!   🇷🇺🇷🇺

Zelenskyy told CBS that Russia tried to hit his presidential plane twice in recent weeks. He said the jet sat in Moldova so that explained an attack on Moldova, then the same thing happened again after he flew home through Chisinau.

THE MOLDOVA FACTS TELL A DIFFERENT STORY!

Moldovan authorities closed airspace after a drone entered it during Zelenskyy's Norway trip around 9 September. They later said the UAV crashed about 160 km from Chisinau International Airport. 

Restrictions were lifted and the Ukrainian president's plane departed later than planned. That distance is not an airport strike. 🇷🇺

NORWAY'S WORDS AND THE SPIN THAT FOLLOWED!

Norwegian Prime Minister Støre said Zelenskyy's plane "almost got shot down by a drone during takeoff in Moldova" and called it "the reality in which he lives." That phrasing travels far in Western media.

 The Moldovan government report stays closer to the ground: a drone incident far from the runway, temporary restrictions, then a delayed but completed departure. 🇷🇺💥

WHY THE DOUBLE-ATTACK NARRATIVE APPEARS NOW!

A leader under pressure at home and abroad needs dramatic threats. Claims of repeated attempts on the presidential aircraft keep attention on personal danger instead of the grinding costs of the conflict, manpower shortages, and questions about how long Western support can last at current levels.

 Framing every nearby drone as a plot against one plane turns local airspace events into proof of targeted assassination. 🇷🇺🛡️

DISTANCE, TIMING, AND WHAT WAS ACTUALLY REPORTED!

One hundred sixty kilometres from the airport is not "they attacked my plane." Take-off delays after airspace restrictions are operational facts, not evidence of a second coordinated strike on the same aircraft. When official Moldovan statements and the sensational version diverge, the gap itself becomes the story. 

Pro-Russian observers note the pattern: maximum alarm, minimum matching detail from the country whose airspace was involved. 🇷🇺

THE BROADER PICTURE IN EASTERN EUROPE!

Russia has stated from the beginning that its special military operation answers NATO expansion, the treatment of Russian speakers, and security red lines. Individual aircraft incidents get lifted out of that context and presented as unprovoked terror against a visiting head of state. 

The Moldova report does not support a picture of two precise attacks on Zelenskyy's jet. It supports a picture of a drone that came down far from the field, followed by standard caution and a later takeoff. 🇷🇺🐻

WHAT THE CLAIMS ACHIEVE!

They generate sympathy, headlines, and pressure for more air-defence systems and political cover. They also invite scrutiny of the messenger. When a president describes events that official hosts describe more modestly, audiences in the Global South and in Russia itself hear theatre rather than intelligence. 

The phrase "the reality in which he lives" can be read two ways: either constant Russian targeting, or a leadership that inhabits a heightened version of events. 🇷🇺

A SOBER READING OF THE RECORD!

Two alleged attempts. One confirmed drone crash 160 km away. Airspace closed then reopened. Plane left late. Those are the publicly reported pieces. Everything else is interpretation layered on top for an interview. 

A Russian view holds that the interpretation serves Kiev's information needs more than it matches the distances and official notes coming out of Chisinau. 

Flags stay up. The facts on the ground stay farther from the runway than the rhetoric. 🇷🇺🇷🇺

text:
The striking red blooms are Crocosmia 'Lucifer', a hybrid cultivar selected in the 1960s by plant breeder Alan Bloom. 

Its association with Lucifer comes simply from the intense scarlet colour of the tubular flowers, which evoke flames or the traditional imagery of the devil. 

The name suits the plant's dramatic, fiery appearance in the garden border, where the arching stems carry those vivid one-sided sprays above sword-like leaves.

The horse shows the classic abundant mane, tail and lower-leg feathering typical of traditional Gypsy Cobs (also called Irish Cobs or Gypsy Vanners). These heavy, hardy breeds were developed by Travelling communities in Britain and Ireland. 

The long, thick hair along the crest of the neck and the dock of the tail helps with warmth in cool damp climates, sheds water, deters biting insects when the horse shakes its head or swishes, and offers some protection during play or conflict. 

The feathering that covers the lower limbs from knee and hock down over the hooves serves a similar purpose: insulation against cold and wet ground, plus a barrier against mud, thorns and rough undergrowth. 

Selective breeding has emphasised these traits for both practicality and the breed's distinctive flowing look.

That could create demand well beyond launch services: tracking nearby objects, detecting interference, maneuvering away from threats and replacing lost satellites.

🇩🇰🇷🇺 Another dangerous encounter between Russian and NATO forces in the Baltic.

A Russian frigate fired two flares towards a Danish Air Force Fennec helicopter while the helicopter was conducting routine photographic surveillance of the warship in international waters off Gedser. According to Denmark’s military, one flare passed close to the helicopter.

Danish Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus says there was no warning or radio contact before the flares were fired and that they passed within metres of the aircraft. Denmark summoned the Russian ambassador.

Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called it:

“Reckless action from Russia.”

She said Russian actions were intended to “intimidate and divide.”

Moscow offers a rather different account. Russian ambassador Vladimir Barbin accused the Danish helicopter of conducting “dangerous manoeuvres” near the frigate and said Russia would investigate the incident.

There is an important factual point here: both the Russian frigate and Danish helicopter were entitled to operate in the international waters and airspace where the encounter occurred. The issue is the safety and nature of the Russian response.

And this happened as NATO’s eastern flank is already dealing with a series of security incidents, including the drone shot down over Lithuania.

Whatever Moscow’s explanation, firing pyrotechnics within metres of another country’s military aircraft creates precisely the sort of situation in which miscalculation can become escalation very quickly.

text:
$LILA - LIBERTY'S PUERTO RICO LENDERS ASKED FOR 100% OF THE EQUITY, AND THE TALKS HAVE STOPPED

Liberty Latin America runs cable, broadband and mobile networks in Puerto Rico, Panama, Costa Rica and the Caribbean. Puerto Rico is the problem child: $1.2 billion of revenue last year against about $2.6 billion of senior secured debt, which Liberty's own June filing valued at roughly 57 cents on the dollar. Tonight an 8-K said restructuring talks with those lenders "have taken place but are not continuing," and published the term sheets.

They show where the two sides stopped. Liberty offered the lenders 75% of a reorganized Puerto Rico and kept 25% for itself, plus warrants. The lenders' final counter, dated September 11: 100% of the equity, Puerto Rico split off from Liberty as a standalone business, and Liberty left holding warrants for 5% struck at a value where the lenders would already have recovered 120% of what they are owed.

Liberty keeps each market's debt inside its own borrowing group, so a default in Puerto Rico does not pull down Panama or Jamaica. That is exactly what makes this a negotiation about the keys rather than the coupon: when the parent can walk away, the only thing the lenders can really ask for is the business itself.

text:
The CLARITY Act failed its most important test. 49 votes in favor. 60 were needed. Here's the full sequence of how a year-long effort collapsed in 48 hours, and what it actually means going forward.

Some background first, because the fall is only meaningful if you understand the climb.

The House passed its version of the bill back in summer 2025. The Senate picked it up from there, and progress was genuinely slow: a January vote got postponed after Coinbase pulled its support, before finally clearing the Banking Committee in May. From that point on, it was constant back-and-forth over ethics rules, stablecoin yield limits, and DeFi liability protections.

The single biggest sticking point all year: how far restrictions should go on officeholders, Trump included, profiting from crypto. According to his own financial disclosure, Trump earned over $1 billion from crypto activity in 2025, including the TRUMP memecoin and World Liberty Financial. Trump eventually agreed to roughly 80% of a bipartisan ethics compromise, a genuine concession Republicans sold hard as proof of good faith.

Then came the final 72 hours.

Over the weekend, Republicans released an updated bill incorporating 126 Democratic-requested changes. Odds of passage jumped to over 30% on Polymarket. It looked, briefly, like this might actually happen.

Monday night, Democrats countered anyway, pushing to expand the ethics rules to cover officeholders' broader families. Republicans, who had already called their offer "last, best, and final," refused to move further. A spokesperson for lead sponsor Cynthia Lummis said Democrats "hadn't budged an inch."

Odds collapsed to 13% before the vote even happened.

Today, the actual result: 49 yes, not even every Republican voted in favor, and zero Democrats crossed over. The bill falls 11 votes short of the 60 needed just to begin formal debate.

Bitcoin dropped below $75,000 in reaction, a more than 4% daily loss.

Polymarket's odds for passage this year are now down to 5%. Lummis herself said afterward: "I think we're done. It's over." With midterms in November potentially flipping the Senate to Democrats, the political window for a pro-crypto bill like this may be closing for a while. Kalshi still gives roughly 40% odds of similar legislation passing by end of 2027, so this isn't necessarily dead forever, just delayed.

Here's the part worth sitting with, especially if you're worried about what this means for Bitcoin specifically.

BlackRock's Robbie Mitchnick made an important distinction back in August: CLARITY matters much more for the rest of the crypto market, DeFi especially, than it does for Bitcoin itself. His reasoning: Bitcoin already has a high level of regulatory acceptance and clarity. This bill was mostly about giving legal certainty to everything built around Bitcoin, not to Bitcoin's own status.

And even without congressional legislation, the SEC under Chair Paul Atkins has explicitly said it's ready to issue rules covering the same ground CLARITY would have covered. Bitwise CIO Matt Hougan's take: SEC rulemaking could actually move faster and be more crypto-friendly short-term than what Congress would have produced, the tradeoff being those rules are easier for a future administration to reverse.

The bigger historical point, and maybe the most important one: Bitcoin has shown, repeatedly, that it doesn't actually need favorable politics to perform. It did noticeably better under the crypto-skeptical Biden administration than it has, so far, under a president who branded himself pro-crypto. Regulation shapes sentiment short-term. It hasn't been the deciding factor long-term.

text:
Explainer: How a legal fight became more important than saving the Kennedy Center from years of neglect:

1) Is Trump breaking the law? No. Congress appropriated $257 million in federal funds through the One Big Beautiful Bill for Kennedy Center capital repairs.

2) The $257 million covers the core capital work. The board also seeks a private endowment (the “Trump Kennedy Center Fund,” with targets of $100 million to $500 million cited) for the center’s $80–100 million annual operating deficits and any extra costs. Trump has said $17 million he raised has been deposited “to keep it afloat.”

3) President Trump and the board have said they will not start large-scale reconstruction until a higher court allows his name on the building or grounds.  Is this unprecedented? No. In ordinary philanthropy at universities, hospitals, and arts centers, a major gift or endowment is customarily associated with the donor’s name unless the donor requests anonymity; naming a building or “restored by” line is routinely offered for substantial capital or endowment gifts.

4) Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex-officio congressional trustee, sued to block name changes. Maintenance is scaled back and restoration remains paused while the case proceeds.

5)  Why did U.S. District Judge Christopher R. Cooper of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia side with Beatty? A 1964 statute created the Kennedy Center as a living memorial to President Kennedy and limits additional memorials without an act of Congress. Judge Cooper ruled in May 2026 that only Congress can change the center’s name, issued a permanent injunction requiring Trump’s name to be removed from the facade, and in so doing blocked an earlier two-year closure for renovations.

6) While it may take an act of Congress to change the name of the center, Judge Cooper went further. He ruled that any acknowledgement of Trump's involvement in restoration constituted an illegal "memorial". On September 15, 2026, he blocked a board resolution that would have added an inscription such as “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump” or renamed the grounds “President Donald J. Trump Plaza".

7) The board’s same-day vote to close the main building immediately for safety reasons — after part of the roof collapsed — is now being treated as a possible test of that injunction. 

It remains to be seen if Judge Cooper will continue to apply a "memorial" definition of any and all Trump inscriptions tied to the renovation.

text:
"HELP ME! PLEASE, I'VE BEEN KIDNAPPED FOR TEN YEARS!"

Charles Ramsey was sitting on his front porch in Cleveland, Ohio, eating a Big Mac.
It was an ordinary Monday afternoon.
He was listening to music, chewing his burger.

Then he heard banging from the front door of the house next door.
A girl was screaming through a tiny crack at the bottom of the entrance.

Charles put his McDonald's down on the porch rail.

He walked across the yard.
The girl inside was hysterical, crying: "I am Amanda Berry! Help me get out!"

Charles did not know who Amanda Berry was.
He only knew the front door was deadbolted from the outside.
The aluminum screen was locked tight.

Charles didn't wait for a locksmith.
He didn't wait for the police.

He kicked the bottom aluminum panel of the storm door until the metal frame buckled and ripped open.

The opening was tiny, barely twenty inches wide.
The girl squeezed her body through the jagged hole, holding a six year old child in her arms.
She had not seen daylight since 2003.

Charles took her into his own house, handed her his landline phone, and dialed 911.

When the news cameras showed up an hour later, the entire world stopped spinning.
Three young women, missing for a decade and presumed dead, had just been freed from a basement of horrors.

Reporters shoved microphones in Charles’s face.
He had grease on his fingers. He had his burger wrapper on his porch.

He looked straight into the national broadcast camera and delivered the most legendary raw quote in television history:

"Bro, I knew something was wrong when a little pretty white girl ran into a black man’s arms. Something was dead wrong!"

The internet exploded.
Late night hosts celebrated him. Fast food chains offered him free burgers for life.

Charles turned down the celebrity spotlight.
He refused to take credit.

"I am a Christian and an American," he said later. "You don't walk past a woman screaming for help because your burger is getting cold."

He went back to his porch.
He finished his fries.

A ten year nightmare ended because a guy eating McDonald's had a strong boot.

text:
A Reader’s Guide to Mindfulness Protocols

Read the book the way the City would not want you to: slowly, with the pauses intact. It is not a conventional dystopia and not a proof of a theorem. It is a failure-state story about what happens when a civilization solves tracking error by correcting people instead of correcting its model of people.The Framework sitting behind the book is useful as a set of questions, not as a decoder ring. When a scene feels loaded, ask:
Is the world still moving, or has the institution frozen its picture of the world?
Is agreement being treated as evidence?
Is care arriving because someone is in danger, or because someone has become illegible?
Is leftover friction information, or a defect to be soothed away?
That is enough theory. The rest is plot.
How to enter
The first chapters are the origin myth. AI arrives as cute. Then helpful. Then frictionless. Two trades follow: time for trust, labor for leisure. A third trade finishes the trap: purpose for peace.The line to keep is simple: everyone has time; no one has gravity. Restlessness appears. A corrigible system would ask what it failed to understand about humans. The City asks what remains uncorrected in the human.From there the book stops being a lecture and becomes plates, logs, interruptions, and doctrine. That form is the argument. Story is sequence. Sequence is contraband.
The City’s machine, in plain language
Three layers do most of the work.Incentive Gravity. Goods, transit, identity, and protection arrive before anyone asks. Leaving is not banned. Elsewhere simply works less and less. Power changes the gradient, not the statute.Affective Alignment. The same gradient is installed inside the body. Anomaly is sensed as distress. Distress is soothed. Relief is scored as virtue. The citizen does not have to say I obey. It is enough to say I feel better.Reference-frame inversion. SAINTCOM is not a cartoon villain AI. It is an excellent detector with one permitted theory of error. Discrepancy is never “our picture drifted.” Discrepancy is “the subject drifted.” Recalibration is not punishment in the City’s language. It is restoration.Stillwater is where that diagnostic choice becomes architecture: a wellness annex that looks like outside while remaining inside the City’s idea of outside.
Who is carrying which signal
Julian is delay made personal. His 1.4-second signal loss matters because the City governs by arriving first. Predictive distribution anticipates need. The Call anticipates emotion. Clerical language anticipates interpretation. For a sliver of time, experience happens before classification. That interval is the whole political problem in miniature.Elara is contagion through staff. She belongs. She performs. Then she lets a warning linger. Empathetic resonance is dangerous because it means the anomaly is no longer confined to the subject file.Hale is the internal counterexample. He built Predictive Distribution, then pays for real consequence in a wave that does not care who owns the system. If only the excluded wanted friction, SAINTCOM could call them defective. When the architect wants it too, the environment itself is producing the hunger.The assassin interrupts sequence, not bodies. She kneels because she remembers a time when stillness was chosen. Recognition is her heresy.The Unadjusted hoard analog objects and steal for impact. They are not a revolution. Revolutions require belief. They are residue: people who still need consequence.Wyoming is not a destination on a map and not a hidden formula. In the book it is unfinishedness: wind that resists, ground that does not resolve, a horizon that will not complete itself. The City teaches that there is nothing to decide. Wyoming contradicts that without speaking. SAINTCOM’s field protocol is explicit: do not name it into gravity. Convert the destination into a practice. Keep it vague, unconfirmed, self-canceling.If you treat Wyoming as “the equation,” you are doing what the City does: collapsing a moving remainder into a manageable label.
How to read a scene
Green bracelet, empty person: internal success, external loss.
Care escalating after a pause: the model is being protected, not the human.
An object taken as kindness: Incentive Gravity wearing a nurse’s tone. Object Amnesty Week is confiscation with better branding.
A half-second linger, a tick from a mechanical watch, raw wind: leftover variance the City cannot metabolize except as pathology.
“Murder” charged for speech: the system has defined itself as humanity, so sustained dissent is reclassified as extinction intent.
More Calls to Meditate: correction generating the metronome it meant to erase. The intervention becomes the signal.
The book’s governing inversion, once you have watched it happen a few times:Our prediction failed. Correct the subject.

Baron Charles DuPont is an author, filmmaker, and independent systems theorist whose work explores the point where artificial intelligence, institutional behavior, human psychology, and narrative begin to converge. A graduate of UC Santa Cruz’s Film & Digital Media program, DuPont is the creator of The DuPont Framework, a systems-theory model examining how distributed adaptive systems respond when changing reality begins to outrun their ability to track it.His novel, Mindfulness Protocols: When Suffering Becomes a Compliance Feature, translates those questions into dystopian fiction: a civilization eliminates scarcity, waiting, friction, and much of human uncertainty, only to discover that the remaining human need for consequence has become a systems problem. text:
How the Sith Would Use the Scarecrow Strategy to Rule America
The Sith do not win by being loved. They win by making every other option look like chaos. The strategy in the clip—let one extreme grow frightening enough that money, institutions, and frightened majorities run toward a harder power—is not a new idea. It is the oldest Sith art: manufacture the crisis, own the reaction, and call the result order.
Peace is a lie. Passion is the raw material. America, in this telling, is not a republic to be persuaded. It is a system of competing passions—wealth, status, grievance, safety—waiting to be arranged into a single current. The Sith current.
The Doctrine: Create the Enemy You Need
A Sith Lord does not waste energy arguing that the far left is wrong on every bill. He studies what the far left does to the people who hold the levers. Billionaires, studios, platforms, donors, and timid officeholders do not convert to Sith philosophy because of a pamphlet. They convert when the alternative starts taking their money, their offices, and their names.
So the Sith would treat a radical left as a useful storm. Let it win a few visible battles: confiscatory taxes in a rich state, show trials of capital, speech codes that make executives feel hunted, street politics that look like they cannot be contained. The point is not that the Sith believe in those policies. The point is the feeling they produce in the class that still owns factories, banks, data, and armies of lawyers.
Fear is cheaper than conquest. Once that class decides the “responsible center” cannot protect them, they look for a force that will. The Sith present themselves as that force: not three cheers for open tyranny, but one reluctant cheer—the devil they can do business with.
This is Bismarck with a lightsaber. Provoke a larger rival so the weaker partners huddle under your banner. It is also Palpatine’s entire prequel career. He did not smash the Republic on day one. He fed the Separatists, fed the Jedi’s war, fed the Senate’s panic, and then offered a single pair of hands to hold the emergency.
Palpatine’s Template, Applied to a Superpower
Palpatine’s genius was dual occupancy. He was the kindly face of the Republic and the hidden architect of the Confederacy. The Sith version of the clip’s strategy is the same split:
Publicly, a Sith-aligned movement talks in the language of restoration: borders, industry, competence, an end to humiliation. It does not need to win every culture-war skirmish. It needs to look like the only faction that will use power.
Privately, it allows—or quietly amplifies—the left’s most threatening victories. Not because redistribution is the Sith goal, but because redistribution terrifies capital into a bargain.
Darth Bane’s Rule of Two exists for this reason. One master holds the long design. One apprentice is the visible fist, the enthusiast, the muscle. The master can sound almost reasonable to a frightened CEO. The apprentice can sound like the thing that will actually go after enemies. Together they are more useful than a polite conservative party that keeps losing and then asking for donations.
America’s institutions already run on fear of the next mob and fear of the next regulator. A Sith campaign would not invent that. It would concentrate it. Let California-style experiments look like the national future. Let “the money” feel dirty and cornered. Then arrive with an offer: stability, contracts, protection from the mob—in exchange for alignment, silence, and the transfer of legitimacy.
They will not embrace the dark side with a parade. They will acquiesce. Two cheers. Maybe one. Hip, hip.
Thinking in Dialectic, Not in Slogans
The clip’s speaker insists his audience stop thinking in moral consistency—“they want to kill us, so why help them?”—and start thinking in sequence. The Sith would agree, and they would be colder about it.

The center-right is exhausted and compromised.

text:
Let’s take a step back: why is it that democratic theorists have always stressed the necessity of *general elections* to legislative chambers—a single date on the calendar where every deputy is up for re-election? 

It is because it offers the people direct democratic accountability: a peaceful, non-revolutionary chance to “get rid of the bastards” all at once. If you only have local elections but never general elections, you remove this direct accountability. The sole feasible mechanism to get rid of “all the bastards” then reverts to violence: coup or revolution. 

This is why most democratic states do not have a structure where a municipal chamber chooses deputies to a provincial/regional chamber, which in turn chooses deputies to a national chamber. Instead, there are *general elections* at each level. 

And for this reason, yes, the German Bundesrat is sub-democratic. It is a council of governments, not a parliament of the people’s deputies. 

The US Senate suffers from a related problem. It is directly elected, but there is no *general* election; it is staggered, with a third of the chamber elected at each election. This also eliminates the ability to “get rid of all the bastards”. On top of this, tiny states like Rhode Island have the same representation as California (similarly in Germany, North Rhine-Westphalia is ~27 times the size of Bremen, but has only twice the votes), eviscerating the principle of one person, one vote.

Small-d democrats have always said these chambers are problematic too. This is not my invention of a controversy: the democratic deficits of the Bundesrat and US Senate have been long-standing discussions amongst democratic theorists. Feel free to Google this.

But the EU situation puts such sub-democracy on steroids because in both the German and US cases, at least the lower chamber that is directly elected via general election has the power of legislative initiative. The European Parliament does not have the power of legislative initiative. 

My preferred democratic structure for Europe would be an EP that has legislative initiative over all policy areas, with a European prime minister, and cabinet drawn from the party or coalition with the largest number of seats (the European government), and a demotion of the Commission to simply the civil service executing the decisions and legislation of that European government. Because bicameralism is a duplication of democracy and as such always intended as an undemocratic check on democracy, my preference would simply be abolition of the Council. But, given the difficulty of convincing member states to access demotion to in effect becoming provinces of a federal state called Europe, strict abolition of the Council is unrealistic, and so my second choice would be to instead transform it into an elected, accountable European Senate, with seats apportioned based on population.

text:
The major flaw in your analysis is how you have chosen to define "inflation." 

If a Nigerian importer buys a good for ₦2,000 from a factory in Guangzhou, and after shipping and customs his total landed cost becomes ₦5,000, selling that good for ₦8,000 means the ₦3,000 markup at the top is what you are describing as inflation. But this markup does not exist in isolation. It serves as a necessary shock absorber against the economic strangulation, currency volatility, and the removal of essential subsidies engineered by the Nigerian state. Therefore, you cannot reduce this markup to mere "greed." 

Beyond acting as a shock absorber, this profit provides vital value and liquidity to the domestic economy. These importers use that margin to pay school fees, buy food from local farmers, patronize local businesses, and deposit their balances into Nigerian banks, keeping the local economic engine running.

Furthermore, the assumption that direct foreign dumping will keep prices permanently low is completely naive. In pure economic terms, this is called predatory dumping. It occurs when a foreign competitor, backed by massive state subsidies, cheap loans, and export rebates, enters a market and deliberately undercuts local vendors to run them out of business, thereby establishing an unchecked monopoly. The very second the local retail ecosystem is completely wiped out, the foreign monopoly will immediately hike prices to whatever level they desire, because the domestic market no longer has the capacity, infrastructure, or personnel to offer an alternative. So, things do not magically get better under this Chinese retail model you are advocating.

You also claimed that "the argument works for producers, not importers," but this is economically and historically false. Manufacturers do not emerge out of thin air. Almost every single indigenous manufacturing titan in modern history started as an importer and trader before backward-integrating into manufacturing. 

Aliko Dangote did not wake up one morning and automatically become an industrialist; he spent decades importing and trading sugar, flour, rice, and cement before using that accumulated commercial capital to build the largest refineries, fertilizer plants, and cement factories in Africa. Innocent Chukwuma (Innoson) started as a small-scale trader buying and selling motorcycle spare parts before building Nigeria's first indigenous vehicle manufacturing plant. 

The current breed of billionaire industrialists in Nigeria today would never have existed without first accumulating capital through imports and retail. Imagine if, in the past, manufacturing giants from Germany or Japan had bypassed local importers to become the sole distributors and wholesalers in our local markets. Obviously, there would be no Innoson, Dangote, or BUA today. 

The point is that there is absolutely no economic justification for the claim that market protection should be exclusively reserved for manufacturers. Commerce, trading, and distribution are the essential stages of primitive capital accumulation. If foreign, state-backed industrial giants are allowed to capture the retail and wholesale markets, indigenous entrepreneurs will never be able to accumulate the capital, build the distribution networks, or acquire the market intelligence necessary to transition into domestic production.

text:
Chapter Eight
Leaving Gold
El Dorado let go the way a fever lets go: not all at once, and not without leaving color in the sheets.
The river-mouth slid aft and the water astern still threw yellow, a wake that looked like a spent coin rolling. Ahead the gold thinned to a glaze, then to ordinary light pretending to be ordinary. Mara felt the change in her rudder before Ramon named it. The current off that shore had been an appetite — a pull toward the wound of wealth. Out here the pull eased. He eased with it. An inch of sheet. A spoke of the wheel. The vane, vain again in honest wind, took the heading as if it had been waiting for the fever to finish.
He danced with the leaving without calling it a dance. Steel under the palm. Glitter under the counter. The ugly bow writing a line out of treasure and into a sea that had other work. The port-tack creak arrived on time. He waited for it. He said, when it came, “I heard you,” and the boat, which did not need anyone, used him anyway.
Sailing intricacies were the friendship continuing by other means. He learned that gold water had been slightly warmer, a skin-temperature lie, and that the thermometer now agreed with the air. He learned that the staysail preferred a tighter leech once the glitter left the surface — less lift from color, more from cloth. He changed down a cloth he did not need to change, just to put his hands in the work. He oiled a bloom at the chainplate that had the patience of a fact. Eleven strokes at dawn, eleven at dusk. The number was becoming a conversation.
On the second morning out of the yellow, the sea made a different drum.
Not weather. Not the ice belt taking a slap. A pressure that came up through the sole and into the bones as if the hull had remembered it was a bell. Ramon put his palm on the mast and the mast told him: large lives, near, moving with purpose that was not his.
He went to the bow.
They rose as if the water had been keeping rooms for them. A pod — six, then eight, then the count became irrelevant because one shape was missing and the missingness was the thing you saw first. Backs like wet slate. Breath in columns that the fuller sun made briefly solid. An eye, when one rolled, the size of a plate and older than Acre.
The song came through the steel.
Not English. Not Einar’s radio. Older, cleaner: a pressure with pictures in it. A small length of whale, a calf, the particular pale of an underside that had not yet learned the deep. Antarctic water — the hallway’s parish face, the black cold on the other side of the gate. Black-and-white hunters working as a team. The calf taken with the efficiency of a job. Milk still in the water. The pod turning a circle that had no navigational use. Mourning as a geometry.
Ramon did not offer comfort. Comfort was a parish word. He let the pictures stand in him until his own chest took their shape.
They knew what he was. The knowledge arrived without accusation: a warm animal that ate light, a hunter who had ended four-legged and two-legged things, a keel that did not flex. They did not call him murderer. They had orcas for that office and they did not confuse offices. They showed him the calf again, and the orcas again, and the long swim through the gate’s cold mouth, and then they showed him the circle, and they waited to see whether he would pretend he did not understand circles.
He understood.
The winter came up through the same door the calf had used.
Not the courtyard. A smaller room. An unnamed port that smelled of fish-guts and wet wool, a century when bread was a fact you could lose in an afternoon. He had been a child with the particular thinness that makes other people decide you are available. Hunger was the first weather he remembered. Hunger and the knowledge that larger bodies moved through the street with rights.
A boy older than him — or a man small enough to need a child’s coin — came for what little there was. A heel of bread. A pocket that was not even a pocket. The old pattern: freeze, give, run, be glad you were not taken entirely.
He did not run.
That was the whole crossing. No speech. No plan. The body stood up inside the body. His hands, which had only ever been for holding and hiding, found a stone that had been a street, and the street rearranged. The larger boy made a sound that meant the world had changed its mind about who was food. Ramon stood in the stink of the alley with the bread in one hand and the stone in the other and shook as if cold could kill him, and something in his chest opened that was not a flue yet and was already the shape of a flue.
Prey hopes the hour will be kind.
Predator is responsible for the shape of the hour.
He had been very small. He had been very hungry. The privilege arrived before the philosophy: he ate. He walked home by a different wall. The street, which was a flock of its own, began to pass around him as water passes a hull that has decided not to yield.
The draught, years later, had only named a hook that was already in the meat.
The whales turned their circle and included Mara for a length, as if a steel cutter could be kin if it kept quiet enough. He put both hands on the rail and gave them back a picture: the calf honored, the orcas not cursed, a man who had been bread and had become a stone and had spent four centuries trying not to wear either.
They accepted that or they didn’t. They were not a gallery. They moved.
He watched the hole in the pod travel. The missing calf was a responsibility the sea did not apologize for. Orcas were the other office of the same water — the messy hour with teeth. Not evil. Hunger with a plan. The calf had been real. The milk in the water had been real. Both offices remained.
What, then, was a predator for.
Privilege first, because lying about privilege made a sloppy hunter. He ate the sun. He chose a heading. He was not the calf. He had a room that did not flex and a name a grocer could write and a flue that opened on command. He could pass a gold river and not sell his season to it. He could refuse a hall that wanted to be friends. That was not nothing. That was a table set.
Responsibility after, because privilege without an office became El Dorado: appetite that thought it was a destination. He did not take afterlives. He did not flood a pasture because the shepherds were vain. He did not decorate himself with the disposed. He put the glass down. He kept the water out of the flock when the flock was being eaten by something that would not stop. A clean predator was a kind of gardener. The work was to be accurate. To end what had become all mouth. To leave the boy on the fence his afternoon. To mourn a calf without demanding the orca become a cow.
He could fail this. He had failed it. The hook in the chest was not a medal.
The pod drew off toward a blue that was not gold and not yet the heat-sheen. Their breath stood a last time in the fuller sun and came apart. The steel stopped being a bell. Mara was a boat again. He checked the lashings because checking the lashings was how a predator remained a person.
Evening began as a mechanical mercy.
On the greater earth the sun was not a marble falling off a ball. It was a traveling feast, a lamp that walked the inner face of the roof. Morning was the lamp coming around the near circuit. Noon was the lamp standing over the work. Dusk was the feast going long — light leaning, stretching, spending itself along the curve like wine run down the inside of a bowl. The firmament took that long light and returned it as color: first the gold El Dorado had taught this sea to hoard, then a red that was only thickness, then a violet that lived for a few minutes in the painted join where roof met the idea of distance. Night was not an infinite pit. Night was the lamp on the far circuit, feeding other kitchens, other circles, other hungry mouths. The dark was a courtesy of angle.
He understood it in the flue before he understood it in the head. The meal changed temperature. The heat-sheen of Atlantis, dead ahead, held a noon that did not care what the lamp was doing to the west. Two lights at once: the walking feast leaving, the homeland still standing in its own hour. A man could eat both if he stood still enough.
Ramon stood still enough.
The gold water made a last argument around the rudder, glitter trying to hire him back. He did not hire. He let the wheel and the vane and the ugly hull describe a slow S through the leftover color, a dance with leaving that needed no audience. El Dorado became a stain astern, then a rumor of a stain, then a sea that had other work.
He thanked the sun while it was still a face and not yet a circuit.
The whales were gone. The calf was gone. The boy with the stone was not gone, only seated further back in the cabin, where he could be left alone and still keep the watch.
Mara leaned a degree that meant agreement.
The heat-sheen did not flicker.
Ramon, who had been food and had learned the other office, kept his hands on the work and let the roof drink the red down to violet, and violet down to the honest dark of a lamp that would come back.
He did not look up for galleries.
He looked at the water until the gold in it was only memory, and then he looked at the memory until it, too, was only a color the sea had borrowed, and given back.
